articles.title: Pakistan v Sri Lanka: tri-series cricket one-day international final – live
articles.summary: Updates on the ODI in Lahore. Play starts 8am GMT Eliminated England beat Sri Lanka | Email Tanya 3rd over: Sri Lanka 10-0 (Avishka 6, Kamindu 4) Shaheen, something less than a towel, more like an ironed pocket hankerchief, tucked into his waistband runs in. Kamindu launches into a pull but just collects a single, but Avishka collects the first boundary of the day to short fine leg. 2nd over: Sri Lanka 5-0 (Avishka 2, Kamindu 3) Pakistan’s James Dean, Naseem Shah, slides in at the other end. Shorter, skiddier. Sri Lanka’s eager beavers have to be content with knocking about a few singles. Continue reading...
articles.content:
49th over: Sri Lanka 321-8 (Asitha 5, Theekshana 7) Naseem with the penultimate over. It’s a mixed bag. He starts with a Arachchige’s wicket, throws in a couple of wides, Theekshana smashes six down the ground and Asitha toe ends four to finish.

Dean Kinsella is back: “Oh no Tanya. It seems I bigged up SL too soon. I thought they were gonna get 350 minimum. I should know by now to say nothing!” Me too, this really has been a limp to the line, but Pakistan haeve been excellent at the death.”

48th over: Sri Lanka 307-7 (Arachchige 15, Theekshana 2) Rauf has been super today. Arachchige pulls him over midwicket for four, but Wellalage is wicket number two. Theekshana ducks into a bouncer and is clattered on the helmet, picks up a couple and passes a concussion test. A slow over rate means only four fielders will be allowed outside the 30 yard circle for Pakistan’s last two overs.

A big fat edge from an attempted upper cut. Wellalage reviews but ultra edge sends him on his way.

47th over: Sri Lanka 299-6 (Arachchige 10, Wellalage 2) Some of the stands at this lovely cricket bowl are nearly full now, the noise levels rising. More so as Liyannage fails to reach the rope. Sri Lanka will pass 300 but not get a sniff of what looked possible at half way.

And another! Liyanage aims for the rope but it is too flat and picks out deep cover.

46th over: Sri Lanka 291-5 (Liyanage 6, Arachchige 3) Shaheen pulls out a fast reversing yorker from his bag of tricks, but Arachchige keeps it out. Immaculate over, just four from it.

45th over: Sri Lanka 285-5 (Liyanage 3, Arachchige 1) An eventful over from Rauf that started with Liyange taking a nasty blow on the back/neck via a wild throw from Shaheen, who apologises immediately. Ooof that must have hurt. Somehow, he’s good to continue. Then the wicket, and just five from the over. Good comeback by Pakistan who now have two new batters at the crease.

Babar keeps his calm to hold onto a ball dropping out of the stratosphere as Rathnayake tries to punt him down the ground.

44th over: Sri Lanka 282-4 (Rathnayake 77, Liyanage 1) Shaheen fancies two in a row, but it’s a terrible review. Three singles follow. Shanaka will be fuming to miss the finale.

A full toss does the business! Shanaka toe-ends it down the ground and straight into the hands of Maaz.

43rd over: Sri Lanka 278-3 ( Rathnayake 75, Shanaka 17) Haris Rauf’s first ball is tonked through extra cover for four by Rathnayake, his third glided away by Shanaka. Super running by Sri Lanka turns one to two. A third four is whipped off Shanaka’s boots. Fifteen from the over.

42nd over: Sri Lanka 263-3 ( Rathnayake 70, Shanaka 7) Shaheen nails three yorkers, but Shanaka isn’t hanging about and with the theatrical swish of a curtain, slams him over long on for six – his tenth of the tournament. Only Harry Brook (12 ) has more. After Kamindu was out, Shaheen raced to shake his hand before he walked off.

One trick too many, as Kamindu tries to scoop a yorker and misses. He reviews, but to no avail, hit on the front boot and umpire’s call. What a debut century!

41st over: Sri Lanka 255-2 (Kamindu 131, Rathnayake 69) Rathnayake is on the charge, sweeping two fours brutally, then Kamindu tucks into a low full toss, one bounce over the rope. Worse, it’s a no ball, but he can only mine one off the free hit, which is pulled straight to long on.

40th over: Sri Lanka 238-2 (Kamindu 126, Rathnayake 58) Naseem Shah with his eighth over, crouches at the top of his run, wipes his sweat away. And there’s the scoop, a reverse, done on the move with style, but only for two. A run-out chance as Kamindu turns back midway down the pitch but the throw misses. Ten overs left as a fading sun has one last blaze.

39th over: Sri Lanka 232-2 (Kamindu 122, Rathnayake 55) Sri Lanka can’t get Arafat away to the rope but still pick up six from the over.

An email drops. Hello Dean Kinsella! “Wow. Just tuned in after following the Saffers destroying Oz this morning. So this is looking like a mammoth total for Sri Lanka. They must be considered serious contenders for the world cup next year. And nothing would please me more.” Wouldn’t that be a cracking narrative? So impressed with their batters, not only the shotmaking but also the composure.

38th over: Sri Lanka 226-2 (Kamindu 120, Rathnayake 52) Dusk is falling over Lahore, the sky a sleepy peach. Kamindu, feet perfectly balanced, pulls Naseem over deep midwicket as if he’s waving away the butler. Rathnayake brings up his fifty with a dab off the hips.

37th over: Sri Lanka 216-2 (Kamindu 113, Rathnayake 49) A tasty short ball from Arafat is pounced on by Rathnayake who pulls it over midwicket.

36th over: Sri Lanka 210-2 (Kamindu 112, Rathnayake 44) Farheem again, long run up, long sleeves. On TMS, Steven Finn says in this scenario England would be looking for the scoops but, as it turns out, Rathnayake doesn’t need to – he flames a short ball to the rope then drives, divinely, on the up, off the back foot to bring up the 100 partnership. The current run rate is just under six an over.

35th over: Sri Lanka 200-2 (Kamindu 111, Rathnayake 35) Haris Rauf seems the most likely, and Shaheen keeps him on. We pause after one ball as Mendis gets an elongated arm massage and a pickle juice. The umpires, in tight-fitting florescent pink, are unimpressed. A top edge flies through where first slip might have hovered.

34th over: Sri Lanka 193-2 (Kamindu 105, Rathnayake 34) With feeling! Upper cuts Faheem for four to bring up three figures, blows out his lips in relief and raises bat in one hand, helmet in the other, to the dressing room where Gary Kirsten leads the applause. Lovely innings, unhurried, but off just 107 balls.

33rd over: Sri Lanka 185-2 (Kamindu 99, Rathnayake 32) After a pause for more drinks, they resume at the Gaddafi stadium. Haris Rauf is brought back with Kamindu just three short of his first ODI century. There he must remain for another over but Rathnayake, nimble footed, hauls four with style.

32nd over: Sri Lanka 176-2 (Kamindu 97, Rathnayake 25) In the Tepal tea lounge, four immaculate looking Pakistan fans serenely sip. Ah, Faheem Ahraf for the first time today. He keeps it tight for five balls, Kamindu pulls his last, which is heading to the rope but well fielded in the deep.

31st over: Sri Lanka 171-2 (Kamindu 94, Rathnayake 23) Pakistan aren’t letting Sri Lanka charge into the distance, but two wides from Shaheen are not ideal in an over that has already leaked six.

30th over: Sri Lanka 164-2 (Kamindu 90, Rathnayake 21) Arafat whistles through an over, four singles from it.

29th over: Sri Lanka 159-2 (Kamindu 88, Rathnayake 19) Shaheen brings himself back on, Pakistan really could do with getting Kamindu out rapidly. The 50 partnership comes up in 44 balls as a huge kite drifts across the ground, in and out of the Lahore mist.

28th over: Sri Lanka 154-2 (Kamindu 86, Rathnayake 15) Kamindu, the most relaxed man in the world, oils his wrists and sends Arafat spilling through the covers for four.

27th over: Sri Lanka 146-2 (Kamindu 80, Rathnayake 14) Naseem pushes his luscious hair back off his face while Shaheen stretches. A fierce bouncer beats Kamindu who just pulls out of a hook in time. Good over.

26th over: Sri Lanka 142-2 (Kamindu 78, Rathnayake 12) Arafat Minhas comes back, ushers his fielders into position with a wave of the hand. Sri Lanka are cautious, respectful.

Australia , incidentally, are four down in the thriller at Cape Town after an over eager Cameron Green runs out Josh Inglis.

25th over: Sri Lanka 138-2 (Kamindu 75, Rathnayake 11) Glorious from Rathnayake, who frying pans Naseem for four off the front foot over mid-on. A pretty drive deserves four but is cut off. The ground is busier now, plenty of people walking up and down the aisles.

24th over: Sri Lanka 128-2 (Kamindu 73, Rathnayake 3) Kamindu gets into position like a whippet and reverse sweeps four past backward point, he follows up with another boundary, this time just gently directed to deep third. Salman, previously economical, is not pleased.

23rd over: Sri Lanka 118-2 (Kamindu 64, Rathnayake 2) Shaheen saves some Haris Rauf for later and brings back Naseem Shah. He nearly picks up Kamindu as well, but a drive lands just short of extra cover.

22nd over: Sri Lanka 114-2 (Kamindu 61, Rathnayake 1) A catch that looks better with each replay! Kamindu picks up four off the last ball of the over with a turn of the bat.

articles.title: South Africa v Australia: third men’s cricket Test, day five – live
articles.summary: Updates from the final day of the series at Newlands Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email 3rd over: Australia 14-2 (Head 9, Green 1) Brave of Green to leave the ball outside off. Similar spot to the one that got Marnus, a touch fuller perhaps. He gets moving from the fifth ball, knocks a single into the off side. 2nd over: Australia 13-2 (Head 9, Green 0) Well, I said that Australia needed Head to take a bite out of the chase first, but wasn’t anticipating that he would lose two partners in the first over. He decides to do his part anyway. Defends three balls from Jansen, then lets loose as he sees width. Misses his first flail, connects cleanly with his second one along the ground, and connects dirty with his third, in the air through the cordon but safe. Two boundaries, but if I were South Africa, I’d happily feed that shot a few times looking for the mistake. Continue reading...
articles.content:
39th over: Australia 62-8 (Cummins 0, Lyon 0) I don’t know how that ball got through Green. So many acres of pad and boot there, bat as well, and somehow it burrowed through a gap. Harmer finishes the over to Lyon, who plays the impulsive sweep first up, then gets his head right and defends.

There it is! A masterstroke from Bavuma. I mean, it was a pretty obvious tactical move, but they still had to do it. Green was trying to avoid facing Harmer, didn’t fancy him with all of that rough outside the off stump, so Bavuma uses the Coetzee over to swing Harmer around to the other end. Green is anxious about it, wants to use his feet to get to the pitch of the ball and defend it from there, like he did well in Sri Lanka a couple of years ago. But that doesn’t help him. He gallops down to block, and can’t make contact anyway. The ball shreds out of the rough, flat and sharp turn, and hits his off stump. Sensational bowling. Game over over over, even though it all but was already.

38th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Ten overs without a run. Coetzee comes on to make Cummins face pace, but Cummins is immaculate, defending everything that he can’t leave.

37th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Jansen replaces Rabada, a little victory for Green there. You’d expect him to bomb Green from left-arm over the wicket, but he only bowls the once bouncer, and Green drops his gloves and spins away, holding his hands protectively to his chest like a kid holding a cake that he doesn’t want to share.

36th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Harmer to Cummins, whose whole approach is to get way out on the front foot to defend. Using his full reach.

“Is the average age of this Australian team now a factor in a really brutal grind of a test match like this one? As well as destroying the careers of an entire generation of young players?”

I think that’s on the hyperbolic side, David Hindle, about the young players. Any national team hopes to have players who are good enough that they keep being involved until well into their 30s. There aren’t a lot of really hard done by players, dominating state cricket and not getting a go. To the contrary, a bunch of pretty average players have had various shots in this team.

As for the effect on this day’s play, fatigue might influence bad shots or bad running decisions, but everyone had a night’s sleep and came into today fresh. Youth didn’t help Connolly decide not to boom a drive at a wide ball turning away from him.

35th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada to Green, who carries on as was foretold. He doesn’t mind some long, slow batting, Green, in a way he’s probably quite enjoying being able to just play and not worry about how to score.

34th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Some repeated themes here. Cummins being hit outside the line and surviving appeals. Cummins squeezing defensive shots away but not taking singles. They’ve scored two runs from one shot in eight overs since lunch.

33rd over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada to Green, who isn’t just dead-batting, he’s trying to keep his rhythm intact by driving the fuller balls. Finds the straight fielders though, doesn’t score. Seam movement seems to have dissipated now that the ball is older.

32nd over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Good over of defence from Cummins that doesn’t have many alarms for five of the balls, but the one that is alarming jumps at him, Harmer hitting the rough, and that’s explosive bounce as well as turn. That kind of misbehaviour will have an impact at some stage.

31st over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada makes Green play at almost everything in that over, which the batter does comfortably enough except for one that goes past the edge.

30th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Harmer to Cummins, who copes with him ok through this over. No run taken when available, Green wants to face Rabada.

29th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Another lbw knocked back, this time Rabada bowling to Green, who is caught on the crease as the ball angles in. Rabada really likes it, he’s roaring, but it struck high, and Green is as tall as they come. Well, except for Jansen.

28th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Pat Cummins batted for a long time in a futile resistance in the final Test the last time he toured here, Johannesburg 2018. That was in the first innings after the top order got blown away, but still. Can do that job, sometimes. I don’t anticipate it today, but he might dig into those memories. He defends through Harmer’s over, and SA waste a review on a ball that hits him outside the line without a true shot played.

27th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) We’re back at it. One slip and a gully for Green facing Rabada, which is interesting. Stack the old cordon, Temba. Runs can’t hurt you now. Right on cue, Green nicks one through the cordon for two. Along the ground, but still.

“Hi Geoff, enjoying your coverage (and the Final Word) as always,” writes Tane Aikman – thank you. “Wonderful to see South Africa as a top test team again, after it was looking pretty dark for them not long ago. As a New Zealander, it’s going to be fascinating to see how Australia responds to this. Goodness knows what the Aussie batting order will be for our tour. I feel the faint, treacherous stirrings of hope...”

Don’t do it, Tane. You know what happens when New Zealand see Australia, no matter how bad that Australian team may be. Unless it’s 1985 and Richard Hadlee is about.

But yes, success for South Africa on the field does keep up the pressure on the rich boards to keep supporting Test cricket outside their own five-Test mutual satisfaction sessions.

“South Africa to nominate Marnus as the Aussie player of the series?” asks Peter Roy. I think he’s the South African player of the series…

Luke Judd writes in. “Of all the contentious calls the selectors have made, I don’t understand the Connolly selection at all. His first class record with the bat is modest at best, and with the ball is frankly poor, albeit small sample size for both. Webster was made to score runs for two shield seasons on the trot before he was brought in. Weatherald put together eighteen months where he was far and away the best bat outside the Australian XI. McSweeney had far more FC form to fall back on. Why have the selectors decided, on the basis of so little, that Connolly is one of the best eleven players in the country? It seems like a vibes call not dissimilar to England with Shoaib Bashir, which they also seem keen to prolong because walking it back is admitting it was wrong. Am I missing something here?”

You’re not missing much. He is a very good prospect with the bat, that much is true: made 90 on debut in a Shield final, which is not nothing, and has a slew of fifties in limited appearances. Plus that big ton in an ODI recently. I still don’t think that makes him a Test pick. They’re picking him based on seeing talent and wanting to back it. But the framing of him as an all-rounder is what makes least sense. You can see how much his teammates rate his bowling given that first Smith in Sri Lanka, and now Cummins here, barely used it.

It’ll be a grim old chat over the soup and sandwiches for the Aussies. A disaster of a session. They’re going to be absolutely pelted by everyone with a passing interest in the sport. South Africa, though, this has been a historic couple of hours for this side. On the mat early in the series, lost that first Test in humiliating style, and they’re been fierce ever since.

26th over: Australia 60-7 (Green 25) Last ball of the over, last ball of the session now as well, and Harmer strikes again. Starc has played with some heart, declining runs and doing his best in defence, but a ball spearing in at his pads causes him concern, thrusting the bat at it while trying to get his feet out of the way. His ankle rolls slightly, he gets the full face of the bat onto the ball, and from there it thuds into his pad and up into the air. Short leg is waiting under it. Harmer has 3 for 5!

25th over: Australia 59-6 (Green 25, Starc 0) If indeed Green is avoiding spin, then South Africa make sure he has to face some. Markram comes on for a bowl. Green drives two runs powerfully to deep cover, then is happy to take a single. So maybe the issue was about Starc facing pace early.

David emails in. “Looking back on this Test, the Australians started off on the wrong foot and it was only Mitchell Starc’s extraordinary intervention at the end of the first day that allowed them to be in front at all. Should never have bowled first with the attack selected, why would they volunteer to face Harmer and Rabada on the final day? Putting their head in the lion’s mouth because of concerns with the batting. Think a large part of that has been insisting on playing Marnus for 12 months past when his form warranted. Has lead to a permanently weak and makeshift top order. You reap what you sow. Time to bite the bullet and reshape the team.”

This batting order has been jumbled and out of sorts for a while now. Opening, three, the confusion between six and seven, have all been problems.

24th over: Australia 56-6 (Green 22, Starc 0) Harmer is teasing Starc’s off stump. Two back-foot defensive punches playing leg side of the ball, trying to keep his pads out of the way, but it leaves the pegs open, and twice Starc misses that shot and Harmer almost bowls him. The last of the over Starc leaves, and Harmer almost bowls him. He’ll get the line right sooner or later, surely.

23rd over: Australia 56-6 (Green 22, Starc 0) I’m neglecting your emails, sorry, things just got too hot in the hot seat. Green takes two runs into the deep, knew he’d have time to get back. More extras for Australia, they’re only a boundary away from becoming second top-scorer, as Coetzee bowls with wild bounce that clears Green and swerves late in the air past the keeper.

22nd over: Australia 50-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Harmer with big turn again, past the edge of Starc’s bat and away for four byes. Yep, they’re dead-batting now. Starc twice hits to deep point and refuses to run. Is that because he doesn’t want to face Coetzee, or Green doesn’t want to face Harmer? Surely Harmer is a massive threat to a left-handed lower order player.

21st over: Australia 46-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Coetzee bowls a maiden. Not many of those for him in this match. What’s the plan for Green from here? Just bat long? I said before play that the draw was unlikely, well it’s absolutely miles away. Perhaps though it’s the only chance Australia have.

20th over: Australia 46-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Another catch goes down! Starc edging Harmer to slip this time, it travels quickly, but Markram isn’t really to blame there, because that ball his clipped the keeper’s glove on the way. Markram is actually moving his hands into the correct spot to take that catch on a fine angle behind the keeper, then the change in direction confounds his efforts, and he nearly wears that ball in the face.

19th over: Australia 46-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Gerald Coetzee, the ultimate afterthought bowler today, finally gets a roll. Green edges him away for a boundary. Lots of pace to work with.

18th over: Australia 42-6 (Green 16, Starc 0) Harmer always shaped as the main day-five influence, then wasn’t required as the first four wickets fell. Now he’s irrevocably shaped this match with a double strike in the 18th over.

No worries, Coop. Your second Test, would you mind coming in at seven with 246 runs to get on day five? Can’t expect much from the junior player in this situation. Harmer gives it flight, offers him a drive, Connolly accepts, and some turn away from the left-hander takes the outside edge.

Capitulation. That is all this is, now. This Australian team is under a fair bit of scrutiny back home already, and it’s going to become intense given the way they’ve thrown this away.

A leg-side nick, leaving a ball that was hitting, a stupid drive against the new ball, a self-inflicted run out, and now a reverse sweep to short fine leg. This ain’t a T20.

17th over: Australia 42-4 (Green 16, Carey 2) Jansen through another over with only a single added.

16th over: Australia 41-4 (Green 16, Carey 1) And so. South Africa were 40 for 4 in Gqeberha, and won. They were 40 for 4 in effect during their third innings here. And now Australia are 40 for 4 in the chase. It’s probably not going to work out for them, though. Carey makes it 41 with his first run.

What have you done, Cam Green? Never a run in that, no need to be pinching singles like it’s the last over of a one-day international. Green pushes Harmer away into the off side and takes off. Inglis does the team thing and responds. He’s quick, but not that quick. The ball limps short leg, barely moving, and Ackerman in that position just has to turn around, run a few steps, pick it up and spin back, firing it over the bails. Rickelton smashes his gloves down on top of the stumps, finding Inglis well short.

15th over: Australia 39-3 (Green 16, Inglis 3) Inglis plays a crisp pull shot, only gets a single for it, but nicely played. And then Green is lucky to survive again! South Africa lose a review into the bargain. Jansen around the wicket angling in, Green pushes forward, and the slightest inside edge, into his front pad, which then deflects the ball millimetres wide of his off stump. The South Africans think it was pad first, so they review. Thus, Green was almost caught behind off the inside edge, almost lbw, and almost bowled, and because of that South Africa lose a review and the batter profits by four runs, because the keeper was too busy appealing to stop the nick going by to the rope.

14th over: Australia 34-3 (Green 12, Inglis 2) Drinks break there, then Harmer continues, and he drops Green off his own bowling! That would have been immense for South Africa. Green drives back straight, but mistimes it, in the air and low to the bowler’s left hand. Harmer gets down and almost fingertips it, maybe touches it into the ground. He’s scooped up a few in this series at slip, and missed one earlier in this match, but now that one goes down from his own work. I have the feeling that more chances will be coming from Harmer, though.

13th over: Australia 32-3 (Green 10, Inglis 2) Jansen continues over the wicket, they’ve got short leg in place, and that man is in play with the left-armer’s angle into the right-hander’s body. Green plays a couple down not too far away from the catcher. Then gets a run into the covers. He has crawled into double figures, staunch resistance so far.

12th over: Australia 31-3 (Green 9, Inglis 2) Here comes Harmer, and he will be key… right on the money first ball! He was picked in this side to bowl to the left-handers, but the big patch of rough is outside the right-hander’s off stump, and he has two of those to deal with. Lands the ball in that rough and it turns sharply into Green’s pad, just outside the line of the off stump. Nearly lbw. Green manages to drive a run to get off strike though.

11th over: Australia 30-3 (Green 8, Inglis 2) Into the leg side goes Inglis for a single, doubling his score. Green finds another. He’s looked very calm so far. Hey, they’re 10 percent of the way to the target, why not?

10th over: Australia 28-3 (Green 7, Inglis 1) Things are starting to settle, as Mulder bowls a maiden to Green. This innings may quickly get down to a grind. But South Africa have the new-ball incisions that have set them up to have the best of that grind.

“Oh no! I started this email at 0/0 but now it’s 2/5 so it’s probably irrelevant now,” says an even less relevant Lachy Zammit. No, that’s not true Lachy, you’re always relevant. “I’m trying to work my way around StatsGuru, looking up famous Australian chases and assessing how experienced those top sevens were. It turns out that searching through stats by yourself is tricky business, so I haven’t worked anything out. What can we say about the importance of the experience in a batting line up for an intense chase?”

Unfortunately there’s no stats category to define how many matches players had previously played at the time of a certain match. The best you can do is find the highest chase scores list, open those scorecards, and eyeball it: see the notable names and the year and figure out how far into their careers they were.

But it’s not necessarily down to experience. Kyle Mayers made a double ton on debut chasing nearly 400. Those great Australian teams didn’t chase a lot of big fourth-innings scores (I remember Hobart 99, and a couple here in South Africa shortly afterwards). They tended to beat teams by big margins, and not need to chase big.

9th over: Australia 28-3 (Green 7, Inglis 1) Rabada continues. Such a smooth mover, delightful to watch. Josh Inglis doesn’t look bothered, after his first-innings century. Works his first run to midwicket. Green takes another.

Ewan Glenton’s email was written before Head’s wicket, but is all the more apt now. “Obviously Travis Head’s place in the team isn’t in doubt, but presumably there’s a bit of debate about whether he should be opening, or made best use of further down the order. Surely a Test opener should be capable of reigning things in when required (I seem to remember Warner - similarly branded an attack-dog opener - was well able to do that). The fact is Aus don’t need a ‘Travis Head special’ today (fun though it would be, of course): they can win this easily scoring at much less about, what, 3.5 an over? And given the rest of their batting isn’t very reliable, to say the least, losing him much before lunch would put them under a load of pressure.”

You have not written an untrue word, Ewan. Killing the chase early can be a good move chasing 200 on a flat track on day two when the other mob have collapsed twice. Less so chasing close to 300 on day five when the other mob have played really well.

8th over: Australia 26-3 (Green 6, Inglis 0) Mulder comes on early, this is interesting. Green isn’t shutting up shop, either, which is probably a good move. Drives him with a lot of punch through the covers, four.

Premonition from David Blackah a few overs ago. “This all swings on Travis Head. If he gets going we are home. I would hate to see it come down to the GOAT holding up an end to save a draw. As the great Rex Mossop used to say, elan elan, toujours elan!”

It has swung on Travis Head, and not Australia’s way. He’s gone home rather than getting anyone home.

7th over: Australia 22-3 (Green 2) And that might be the ball game! What an over, it’s a journey from start to finish. Walk through it with me.

A defensive shot from Green gets him a run into the off side, then Rabada goes back to tormenting Head. Seam movement again, angled in at Head from around the wicket, then it decks away. So noticeable that this ball is seaming where barely a delivery moved sideways off the surface in the first four days. Head gets control of himself next ball, and rather than throwing the bat he places it, driving in front of point in lovely style for four. But that’s as far as his day will go. Rabada goes yorker, curling in, and Head just about keeps it out, lots of toe of the bat, which twists in his hands. Then the sixth ball is the telling blow, pushed a little wider, a fuller length that yet is not a half volley, and Head drives because Head drives, big edge, and Jansen in the gully buckets it in front of his face.

6th over: Australia 17-2 (Head 10, Green 1) Jansen thumps a ball from over the wicket into the middle of Head’s pad, on an angle so there’s no dismissal risk, but it’s such a hefty blow that it takes a lot of pace out of the ball, keeping the resulting leg byes to two rather than four. That’s the only good news for Australia right now.

Muhammad Najib writes in. “Who says Test cricket is dead? It’s keeping the lights on here in Seattle. This final day reminds me of several iconic matches at once: Ashes 2005 second and third Tests both; Ashes 2006 when Mike Hussey scored the winning runs, then Travis Head’s century in the last Ashes. Whatever happens happens. It’s a day of pressure and whoever handles pressure best… All I want to see is a Marnus ton, so we keep listening to his onfield commentary with Gaz bowling on the other end.”

5th over: Australia 15-2 (Head 10, Green 1) Travis! You cad. Another whistling cut shot that meets nothing but nitrogen and oxygen molecules. Misses that one, the Rabada gets it to seam again and beats a straighter edge. Head changes his tune and instead dashes a single wide of mid on.

“Morning Geoff,” writes Simon McMahon. “Very much looking forward to this. Final day of the series, two champion teams, result in the balance. Test cricket, eh? Let’s play!”

4th over: Australia 14-2 (Head 9, Green 1) A maiden from Jansen to Green, the giants battling one another, and Jansen nearly bowls him, mind you. A short ball that has Green hopping, plays it down into the turf, and it rolls back past his stumps.

3rd over: Australia 14-2 (Head 9, Green 1) Brave of Green to leave the ball outside off. Similar spot to the one that got Marnus, a touch fuller perhaps. He gets moving from the fifth ball, knocks a single into the off side.

2nd over: Australia 13-2 (Head 9, Green 0) Well, I said that Australia needed Head to take a bite out of the chase first, but wasn’t anticipating that he would lose two partners in the first over. He decides to do his part anyway. Defends three balls from Jansen, then lets loose as he sees width. Misses his first flail, connects cleanly with his second one along the ground, and connects dirty with his third, in the air through the cordon but safe. Two boundaries, but if I were South Africa, I’d happily feed that shot a few times looking for the mistake.

1st over: Australia 5-2 (Head 1) It had seemed such a quiet start. Travis Head took the first ball, defending crisply with a perfectly vertical bat down the line of off stump. Dolloped away his leg-side run from the second. Then Renshaw gone from the third. He had moved across a long way before glancing, is the main criticism – people always say it’s unlucky to be caught down leg, but I’m not sure why. It’s a mistimed shot, and moving across does bring the keeper into play, it increases the range of angles off the bat that could be short.

Anyway, then Labuschagne arrived, nicked a ball for four, survived a curling yorker, and tried to leave the length ball.

If you’re confused by the score at the top, that’s global style, five runs and two wickets.

We said he needed eight, he might take all 10! Marnus Labuschagne is done as a Test cricketer, surely, surely, surely. Not many uglier dismissals than that, as he leaves a ball that jags back and hits his pad. Well outside the line of the stumps, but there’s no shot offered, and Dick Kettleborough pops up the finger without demur. Marnus has one last umpire review for old time’s sake, and it shows what the live vision suggested: umpire’s call on hitting the outside the off-stump. That’s good enough to bowl a player, so it should be good enough to trap them as well. Australia struggled to get seam movement yesterday, but with this brand new ball, Rabada does, and irresistibly shapes this match.

Only seven to go, then, Kagiso! One of the blows that Australia could least afford. Renshaw their best long-innings performer, on the evidence of this series. Totally innocuous, ball on leg stump, he’s on the move looking to glance as he’s done throughout this tour, and he nicks it down the leg-side to the keeper. Out first ball, after Head played a similar glance to get off strike. Labuschagne is into the fire in the first over!

Kagiso Rabada to start us off… if he takes eight wickets today, he’ll match Dennis Lillee’s 355 Test wickets. Dare to dream.

Send me an email, let’s do this with company. Gervase Greene is out of the blocks early.

“I have not looked forward to an evening in front of the telly in a lifetime. (Maybe the last day, the Oval, 2005… There’s more sub-plots than an Agatha Christie. Marnus? Trav’s spot in the order? Cam Green? Who the hell - and how the hell - we open? The call to send them in…? Wow.”

I’m not sure if that means Gervase has never looked forward more to an evening in front of the telly, or has never looked forward to one full stop. Either sentiment would be fair.

Now, I bet there is a good chance that you are saying, or that somebody will in your hearing today say, that it’s a tough blow for Australia that they don’t have Steve Smith playing. Their great batting champion, tough chase without him, et cetera, et cetera.

Not so, King of Siam, because Steve Smith in his long and remarkable career has barely made a run in the fourth innings of a Test, and barely faced a ball on the fifth day. He wins games early, and has never notably won or saved one late. I did the analysis a while back, and it still holds. Interesting to delve into the detail of how a career works.

Long story short, for this job Australia are better off with other players doing it.

What happened yesterday? Great question. A fine day of Test cricket, that’s what. But you want to know more. I know a guy who does match reports for The Guardian, let me hook you up.

It would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away. Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1,678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for four in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for four in the third innings here , and now have a great chance to do the same.

I have been saying it every day throughout this match, and most of the days throughout this series, but I can say it with truth one more time: what a beautifully set up contest. The previous 14 days all come down to this. Day five, third Test, Cape Town, where in series terms winner will take all.

Australia must chase 288 to win. South Africa must take 10 wickets. The weather is fine, so the draw is not really on the cards, unless there’s a big early collapse followed by a defensive effort. In the main, if this Australian team bats 90 overs, they’ll score what needs to be scored in the course of that.

My instinct says South Africa, however. It was not easy to bat out there on day four, which highlights just how well Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder did so for their twin centuries. Starting was difficult. There was big turn on offer, and SA have a quality spinner as well as their quality quicks. I think 288 looks right this second like a reasonable target but will rapidly look a much taller one with a couple of wickets.

The key, as so often for Australia in recent times, is Travis Head. If he can make a chunky score up front, that might put the others in the frame. If he goes early, which is always a strong chance given his playing style, that might be that.

Another belter of a day awaits. Let’s take one more turn through the garden.
paragraphs: 39th over: Australia 62-8 (Cummins 0, Lyon 0) I don’t know how that ball got through Green. So many acres of pad and boot there, bat as well, and somehow it burrowed through a gap. Harmer finishes the over to Lyon, who plays the impulsive sweep first up, then gets his head right and defends.

There it is! A masterstroke from Bavuma. I mean, it was a pretty obvious tactical move, but they still had to do it. Green was trying to avoid facing Harmer, didn’t fancy him with all of that rough outside the off stump, so Bavuma uses the Coetzee over to swing Harmer around to the other end. Green is anxious about it, wants to use his feet to get to the pitch of the ball and defend it from there, like he did well in Sri Lanka a couple of years ago. But that doesn’t help him. He gallops down to block, and can’t make contact anyway. The ball shreds out of the rough, flat and sharp turn, and hits his off stump. Sensational bowling. Game over over over, even though it all but was already.
38th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Ten overs without a run. Coetzee comes on to make Cummins face pace, but Cummins is immaculate, defending everything that he can’t leave.

37th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Jansen replaces Rabada, a little victory for Green there. You’d expect him to bomb Green from left-arm over the wicket, but he only bowls the once bouncer, and Green drops his gloves and spins away, holding his hands protectively to his chest like a kid holding a cake that he doesn’t want to share.
36th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Harmer to Cummins, whose whole approach is to get way out on the front foot to defend. Using his full reach.
“Is the average age of this Australian team now a factor in a really brutal grind of a test match like this one? As well as destroying the careers of an entire generation of young players?”

I think that’s on the hyperbolic side, David Hindle, about the young players. Any national team hopes to have players who are good enough that they keep being involved until well into their 30s. There aren’t a lot of really hard done by players, dominating state cricket and not getting a go. To the contrary, a bunch of pretty average players have had various shots in this team.

As for the effect on this day’s play, fatigue might influence bad shots or bad running decisions, but everyone had a night’s sleep and came into today fresh. Youth didn’t help Connolly decide not to boom a drive at a wide ball turning away from him.

35th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada to Green, who carries on as was foretold. He doesn’t mind some long, slow batting, Green, in a way he’s probably quite enjoying being able to just play and not worry about how to score.

34th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Some repeated themes here. Cummins being hit outside the line and surviving appeals. Cummins squeezing defensive shots away but not taking singles. They’ve scored two runs from one shot in eight overs since lunch.

33rd over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada to Green, who isn’t just dead-batting, he’s trying to keep his rhythm intact by driving the fuller balls. Finds the straight fielders though, doesn’t score. Seam movement seems to have dissipated now that the ball is older.

32nd over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Good over of defence from Cummins that doesn’t have many alarms for five of the balls, but the one that is alarming jumps at him, Harmer hitting the rough, and that’s explosive bounce as well as turn. That kind of misbehaviour will have an impact at some stage.
31st over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Rabada makes Green play at almost everything in that over, which the batter does comfortably enough except for one that goes past the edge.
30th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Harmer to Cummins, who copes with him ok through this over. No run taken when available, Green wants to face Rabada.

29th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Another lbw knocked back, this time Rabada bowling to Green, who is caught on the crease as the ball angles in. Rabada really likes it, he’s roaring, but it struck high, and Green is as tall as they come. Well, except for Jansen.

28th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) Pat Cummins batted for a long time in a futile resistance in the final Test the last time he toured here, Johannesburg 2018. That was in the first innings after the top order got blown away, but still. Can do that job, sometimes. I don’t anticipate it today, but he might dig into those memories. He defends through Harmer’s over, and SA waste a review on a ball that hits him outside the line without a true shot played.

27th over: Australia 62-7 (Green 27, Cummins 0) We’re back at it. One slip and a gully for Green facing Rabada, which is interesting. Stack the old cordon, Temba. Runs can’t hurt you now. Right on cue, Green nicks one through the cordon for two. Along the ground, but still.

“Hi Geoff, enjoying your coverage (and the Final Word) as always,” writes Tane Aikman – thank you. “Wonderful to see South Africa as a top test team again, after it was looking pretty dark for them not long ago. As a New Zealander, it’s going to be fascinating to see how Australia responds to this. Goodness knows what the Aussie batting order will be for our tour. I feel the faint, treacherous stirrings of hope...”
Don’t do it, Tane. You know what happens when New Zealand see Australia, no matter how bad that Australian team may be. Unless it’s 1985 and Richard Hadlee is about.
But yes, success for South Africa on the field does keep up the pressure on the rich boards to keep supporting Test cricket outside their own five-Test mutual satisfaction sessions.
“South Africa to nominate Marnus as the Aussie player of the series?” asks Peter Roy. I think he’s the South African player of the series…

Luke Judd writes in. “Of all the contentious calls the selectors have made, I don’t understand the Connolly selection at all. His first class record with the bat is modest at best, and with the ball is frankly poor, albeit small sample size for both. Webster was made to score runs for two shield seasons on the trot before he was brought in. Weatherald put together eighteen months where he was far and away the best bat outside the Australian XI. McSweeney had far more FC form to fall back on. Why have the selectors decided, on the basis of so little, that Connolly is one of the best eleven players in the country? It seems like a vibes call not dissimilar to England with Shoaib Bashir, which they also seem keen to prolong because walking it back is admitting it was wrong. Am I missing something here?”

You’re not missing much. He is a very good prospect with the bat, that much is true: made 90 on debut in a Shield final, which is not nothing, and has a slew of fifties in limited appearances. Plus that big ton in an ODI recently. I still don’t think that makes him a Test pick. They’re picking him based on seeing talent and wanting to back it. But the framing of him as an all-rounder is what makes least sense. You can see how much his teammates rate his bowling given that first Smith in Sri Lanka, and now Cummins here, barely used it.

It’ll be a grim old chat over the soup and sandwiches for the Aussies. A disaster of a session. They’re going to be absolutely pelted by everyone with a passing interest in the sport. South Africa, though, this has been a historic couple of hours for this side. On the mat early in the series, lost that first Test in humiliating style, and they’re been fierce ever since.

26th over: Australia 60-7 (Green 25) Last ball of the over, last ball of the session now as well, and Harmer strikes again. Starc has played with some heart, declining runs and doing his best in defence, but a ball spearing in at his pads causes him concern, thrusting the bat at it while trying to get his feet out of the way. His ankle rolls slightly, he gets the full face of the bat onto the ball, and from there it thuds into his pad and up into the air. Short leg is waiting under it. Harmer has 3 for 5!

25th over: Australia 59-6 (Green 25, Starc 0) If indeed Green is avoiding spin, then South Africa make sure he has to face some. Markram comes on for a bowl. Green drives two runs powerfully to deep cover, then is happy to take a single. So maybe the issue was about Starc facing pace early.

David emails in. “Looking back on this Test, the Australians started off on the wrong foot and it was only Mitchell Starc’s extraordinary intervention at the end of the first day that allowed them to be in front at all. Should never have bowled first with the attack selected, why would they volunteer to face Harmer and Rabada on the final day? Putting their head in the lion’s mouth because of concerns with the batting. Think a large part of that has been insisting on playing Marnus for 12 months past when his form warranted. Has lead to a permanently weak and makeshift top order. You reap what you sow. Time to bite the bullet and reshape the team.”
This batting order has been jumbled and out of sorts for a while now. Opening, three, the confusion between six and seven, have all been problems.

24th over: Australia 56-6 (Green 22, Starc 0) Harmer is teasing Starc’s off stump. Two back-foot defensive punches playing leg side of the ball, trying to keep his pads out of the way, but it leaves the pegs open, and twice Starc misses that shot and Harmer almost bowls him. The last of the over Starc leaves, and Harmer almost bowls him. He’ll get the line right sooner or later, surely.

23rd over: Australia 56-6 (Green 22, Starc 0) I’m neglecting your emails, sorry, things just got too hot in the hot seat. Green takes two runs into the deep, knew he’d have time to get back. More extras for Australia, they’re only a boundary away from becoming second top-scorer, as Coetzee bowls with wild bounce that clears Green and swerves late in the air past the keeper.

22nd over: Australia 50-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Harmer with big turn again, past the edge of Starc’s bat and away for four byes. Yep, they’re dead-batting now. Starc twice hits to deep point and refuses to run. Is that because he doesn’t want to face Coetzee, or Green doesn’t want to face Harmer? Surely Harmer is a massive threat to a left-handed lower order player.

20th over: Australia 46-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Another catch goes down! Starc edging Harmer to slip this time, it travels quickly, but Markram isn’t really to blame there, because that ball his clipped the keeper’s glove on the way. Markram is actually moving his hands into the correct spot to take that catch on a fine angle behind the keeper, then the change in direction confounds his efforts, and he nearly wears that ball in the face.
19th over: Australia 46-6 (Green 20, Starc 0) Gerald Coetzee, the ultimate afterthought bowler today, finally gets a roll. Green edges him away for a boundary. Lots of pace to work with.

And now Australia are 40 for 4 in the chase. It’s probably not going to work out for them, though. Carey makes it 41 with his first run.

South Africa lose a review into the bargain. Jansen around the wicket angling in, Green pushes forward, and the slightest inside edge, into his front pad, which then deflects the ball millimetres wide of his off stump. The South Africans think it was pad first, so they review. Thus, Green was almost caught behind off the inside edge, almost lbw, and almost bowled, and because of that South Africa lose a review and the batter profits by four runs, because the keeper was too busy appealing to stop the nick going by to the rope.

14th over: Australia 34-3 (Green 12, Inglis 2) Drinks break there, then Harmer continues, and he drops Green off his own bowling! That would have been immense for South Africa. Green drives back straight, but mistimes it, in the air and low to the bowler’s left hand. Harmer gets down and almost fingertips it, maybe touches it into the ground. He’s scooped up a few in this series at slip, and missed one earlier in this match, but now that one goes down from his own work. I have the feeling that more chances will be coming from Harmer, though.

13th over: Australia 32-3 (Green 10, Inglis 2) Jansen continues over the wicket, they’ve got short leg in place, and that man is in play with the left-armer’s angle into the right-hander’s body. Green plays a couple down not too far away from the catcher. Then gets a run into the covers. He has crawled into double figures, staunch resistance so far.

12th over: Australia 31-3 (Green 9, Inglis 2) Here comes Harmer, and he will be key… right on the money first ball! He was picked in this side to bowl to the left-handers, but the big patch of rough is outside the right-hander’s off stump, and he has two of those to deal with. Lands the ball in that rough and it turns sharply into Green’s pad, just outside the line of the off stump. Nearly lbw. Green manages to drive a run to get off strike though.

11th over: Australia 30-3 (Green 8, Inglis 2) Into the leg side goes Inglis for a single, doubling his score. Green finds another. He’s looked very calm so far. Hey, they’re 10 percent of the way to the target, why not?

10th over: Australia 28-3 (Green 7, Inglis 1) Things are starting to settle, as Mulder bowls a maiden to Green. This innings may quickly get down to a grind. But South Africa have the new-ball incisions that have set them up to have the best of that grind.

“Oh no! I started this email at 0/0 but now it’s 2/5 so it’s probably irrelevant now,” says an even less relevant Lachy Zammit. No, that’s not true Lachy, you’re always relevant. “I’m trying to work my way around StatsGuru, looking up famous Australian chases and assessing how experienced those top sevens were. It turns out that searching through stats by yourself is tricky business, so I haven’t worked anything out. What can we say about the importance of the experience in a batting line up for an intense chase?”

Unfortunately there’s no stats category to define how many matches players had previously played at the time of a certain match. The best you can do is find the highest chase scores list, open those scorecards, and eyeball it: see the notable names and the year and figure out how far into their careers they were.

But it’s not necessarily down to experience. Kyle Mayers made a double ton on debut chasing nearly 400. Those great Australian teams didn’t chase a lot of big fourth-innings scores (I remember Hobart 99, and a couple here in South Africa shortly afterwards). They tended to beat teams by big margins, and not need to chase big.

9th over: Australia 28-3 (Green 7, Inglis 1) Rabada continues. Such a smooth mover, delightful to watch. Josh Inglis doesn’t look bothered, after his first-innings century. Works his first run to midwicket. Green takes another.

Ewan Glenton’s email was written before Head’s wicket, but is all the more apt now. “Obviously Travis Head’s place in the team isn’t in doubt, but presumably there’s a bit of debate about whether he should be opening, or made best use of further down the order. Surely a Test opener should be capable of reigning things in when required (I seem to remember Warner - similarly branded an attack-dog opener - was well able to do that). The fact is Aus don’t need a ‘Travis Head special’ today (fun though it would be, of course): they can win this easily scoring at much less about, what, 3.5 an over? And given the rest of their batting isn’t very reliable, to say the least, losing him much before lunch would put them under a load of pressure.”

You have not written an untrue word, Ewan. Killing the chase early can be a good move chasing 200 on a flat track on day two when the other mob have collapsed twice. Less so chasing close to 300 on day five when the other mob have played really well.

8th over: Australia 26-3 (Green 6, Inglis 0) Mulder comes on early, this is interesting. Green isn’t shutting up shop, either, which is probably a good move. Drives him with a lot of punch through the covers, four.

Premonition from David Blackah a few overs ago. “This all swings on Travis Head. If he gets going we are home. I would hate to see it come down to the GOAT holding up an end to save a draw. As the great Rex Mossop used to say, elan elan, toujours elan!”
It has swung on Travis Head, and not Australia’s way. He’s gone home rather than getting anyone home.
7th over: Australia 22-3 (Green 2) And that might be the ball game! What an over, it’s a journey from start to finish. Walk through it with me.

A defensive shot from Green gets him a run into the off side, then Rabada goes back to tormenting Head. Seam movement again, angled in at Head from around the wicket, then it decks away. So noticeable that this ball is seaming where barely a delivery moved sideways off the surface in the first four days. Head gets control of himself next ball, and rather than throwing the bat he places it, driving in front of point in lovely style for four. But that’s as far as his day will go. Rabada goes yorker, curling in, and Head just about keeps it out, lots of toe of the bat, which twists in his hands. Then the sixth ball is the telling blow, pushed a little wider, a fuller length that yet is not a half volley, and Head drives because Head drives, big edge, and Jansen in the gully buckets it in front of his face.

6th over: Australia 17-2 (Head 10, Green 1) Jansen thumps a ball from over the wicket into the middle of Head’s pad, on an angle so there’s no dismissal risk, but it’s such a hefty blow that it takes a lot of pace out of the ball, keeping the resulting leg byes to two rather than four. That’s the only good news for Australia right now.

Muhammad Najib writes in. “Who says Test cricket is dead? It’s keeping the lights on here in Seattle. This final day reminds me of several iconic matches at once: Ashes 2005 second and third Tests both; Ashes 2006 when Mike Hussey scored the winning runs, then Travis Head’s century in the last Ashes. Whatever happens happens. It’s a day of pressure and whoever handles pressure best… All I want to see is a Marnus ton, so we keep listening to his onfield commentary with Gaz bowling on the other end.”

5th over: Australia 15-2 (Head 10, Green 1) Travis! You cad. Another whistling cut shot that meets nothing but nitrogen and oxygen molecules. Misses that one, the Rabada gets it to seam again and beats a straighter edge. Head changes his tune and instead dashes a single wide of mid on.
“Morning Geoff,” writes Simon McMahon. “Very much looking forward to this. Final day of the series, two champion teams, result in the balance. Test cricket, eh? Let’s play!”

4th over: Australia 14-2 (Head 9, Green 1) A maiden from Jansen to Green, the giants battling one another, and Jansen nearly bowls him, mind you. A short ball that has Green hopping, plays it down into the turf, and it rolls back past his stumps.

3rd over: Australia 14-2 (Head 9, Green 1) Brave of Green to leave the ball outside off. Similar spot to the one that got Marnus, a touch fuller perhaps. He gets moving from the fifth ball, knocks a single into the off side.

2nd over: Australia 13-2 (Head 9, Green 0) Well, I said that Australia needed Head to take a bite out of the chase first, but wasn’t anticipating that he would lose two partners in the first over. He decides to do his part anyway. Defends three balls from Jansen, then lets loose as he sees width. Misses his first flail, connects cleanly with his second one along the ground, and connects dirty with his third, in the air through the cordon but safe. Two boundaries, but if I were South Africa, I’d happily feed that shot a few times looking for the mistake.

1st over: Australia 5-2 (Head 1) It had seemed such a quiet start. Travis Head took the first ball, defending crisply with a perfectly vertical bat down the line of off stump. Dolloped away his leg-side run from the second. Then Renshaw gone from the third. He had moved across a long way before glancing, is the main criticism – people always say it’s unlucky to be caught down leg, but I’m not sure why. It’s a mistimed shot, and moving across does bring the keeper into play, it increases the range of angles off the bat that could be short.
Anyway, then Labuschagne arrived, nicked a ball for four, survived a curling yorker, and tried to leave the length ball.
If you’re confused by the score at the top, that’s global style, five runs and two wickets.

We said he needed eight, he might take all 10! Marnus Labuschagne is done as a Test cricketer, surely, surely, surely. Not many uglier dismissals than that, as he leaves a ball that jags back and hits his pad. Well outside the line of the stumps, but there’s no shot offered, and Dick Kettleborough pops up the finger without demur. Marnus has one last umpire review for old time’s sake, and it shows what the live vision suggested: umpire’s call on hitting the outside the off-stump. That’s good enough to bowl a player, so it should be good enough to trap them as well. Australia struggled to get seam movement yesterday, but with this brand new ball, Rabada does, and irresistibly shapes this match.

Only seven to go, then, Kagiso! One of the blows that Australia could least afford. Renshaw their best long-innings performer, on the evidence of this series. Totally innocuous, ball on leg stump, he’s on the move looking to glance as he’s done throughout this tour, and he nicks it down the leg-side to the keeper. Out first ball, after Head played a similar glance to get off strike. Labuschagne is into the fire in the first over!
Kagiso Rabada to start us off… if he takes eight wickets today, he’ll match Dennis Lillee’s 355 Test wickets. Dare to dream.
Send me an email, let’s do this with company. Gervase Greene is out of the blocks early.

“I have not looked forward to an evening in front of the telly in a lifetime. (Maybe the last day, the Oval, 2005… There’s more sub-plots than an Agatha Christie. Marnus? Trav’s spot in the order? Cam Green? Who the hell - and how the hell - we open? The call to send them in…? Wow.”
I’m not sure if that means Gervase has never looked forward more to an evening in front of the telly, or has never looked forward to one full stop. Either sentiment would be fair.

Now, I bet there is a good chance that you are saying, or that somebody will in your hearing today say, that it’s a tough blow for Australia that they don’t have Steve Smith playing. Their great batting champion, tough chase without him, et cetera, et cetera.

Not so, King of Siam, because Steve Smith in his long and remarkable career has barely made a run in the fourth innings of a Test, and barely faced a ball on the fifth day. He wins games early, and has never notably won or saved one late. I did the analysis a while back, and it still holds. Interesting to delve into the detail of how a career works.
Long story short, for this job Australia are better off with other players doing it.
What happened yesterday? Great question. A fine day of Test cricket, that’s what. But you want to know more. I know a guy who does match reports for The Guardian, let me hook you up.

It would be unfair to say that Australia let a winning position slip on the fourth day of the third Test at Cape Town, only because that would undersell how Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder prised it away. Australia’s vaunted four bowlers, owners of 1,674 wickets at day’s beginning, could only raise that to 1,678 by day’s end. In the process, a lead of 40 became 287. South Africa had been 40 for four in the first innings at Gqeberha and bounced back to win; they were effectively 40 for four in the third innings here , and now have a great chance to do the same.

I have been saying it every day throughout this match, and most of the days throughout this series, but I can say it with truth one more time: what a beautifully set up contest. The previous 14 days all come down to this. Day five, third Test, Cape Town, where in series terms winner will take all.

Australia must chase 288 to win. South Africa must take 10 wickets. The weather is fine, so the draw is not really on the cards, unless there’s a big early collapse followed by a defensive effort. In the main, if this Australian team bats 90 overs, they’ll score what needs to be scored in the course of that.

My instinct says South Africa, however. It was not easy to bat out there on day four, which highlights just how well Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder did so for their twin centuries. Starting was difficult. There was big turn on offer, and SA have a quality spinner as well as their quality quicks. I think 288 looks right this second like a reasonable target but will rapidly look a much taller one with a couple of wickets.

The key, as so often for Australia in recent times, is Travis Head. If he can make a chunky score up front, that might put the others in the frame. If he goes early, which is always a strong chance given his playing style, that might be that.
Another belter of a day awaits. Let’s take one more turn through the garden.

So many acres of pad and boot there, bat as well, and somehow it burrowed through a gap.
Harmer finishes the over to Lyon, who plays the impulsive sweep first up, then gets his head right and defends.
The article says green is unrelated to the main events described.

articles.summary: Bruno Fernandes and Estêvão returned to the Manchester United and Chelsea lineups ahead of their meeting at Stamford Bridge Here is the article in question and a snippet of Andy’s stat action … Mac Allister’s sense of responsibility extends to implementing Iraola’s instructions for his new team. Figures from Opta show the midfielder is winning more tackles per Premier League game this season – 2.3 on average compared to 1.8 last season; winning more duels (4.8 from 3.8); winning more aerial duels (0.9 from 0.6) and winning more possession (5.6 on average compared to 3.8). He is sacrificing the offensive side of his game to bring more aggression and organisation to the defensive aspect, and his touches in the opposition box, chances created, goals and assists are all down on last season as a consequence. Not that Iraola is complaining. Continue reading...
articles.content:
That’s all from Matchday Live today. Thanks for your comments and emails – be sure to come back tomorrow for more of the same.

Good of Michael Carrick to get into the Halloween Spirit by getting off the coach dressed as a dead man walking

I’ll leave you in the hands of Scott Murray for Chelsea v Manchester United in the Premier League .

Everton (4-4-2): Brosnan; Blundell, Layzell, Ishikawa, Kitagawa; Pacheco, Wheeler, Mace, Vignola; Momiki, Van Gool. Subs: Foster, Cain, Rantala, Mouchon, Finnigan, Galli, Silcock.

Man Utd (4-2-3-1): Tullis-Joyce; Lundkvist, Le Tissier, Janssen, Sandberg; Zigiotti Olme, Miyazawa; Park, Toone, Medina; Terland. Subs: Leitzig, Ildhusoy, Awujo, Rivière, Bernal, Wangerheim, Bah, Schüller, Griffiths.

Today will be an interesting one. I think I read a stat that we hadn’t beat Brum since 1941 and until that Cardiff game Birmingham were in incredibly good form, hadn’t lost in 15 games. Can’t see us getting past them but we’re in a healthy enough position for now.

Team news from Lincoln v Birmingham (12.30pm GMT kick-off) in the Championship is in.

Lincoln (4-2-3-1): Wickens; Coubis, Elerewe, Bradley, Reach; Konak, Varfolomeyev; Hackett, Jefferies, House; Ladefoged. Subs: Gauci, Towler, Bayliss, Street, Olaofe, Elder, Ogbene, Oyegoke, Draper.

Birmingham (4-2-3-1): Beadle; Laird, Neumann, Klarer, Cochrane; Iwata, Solís; Roberts, Stansfield, Millar; Priske. Subs: Allsop, Buchanan, Vicente, Gray, Bird, Gardner-Hickman, Samuel, Vázquez, Ducksch.

There’s a thick layer of low-hanging cloud over Goodison Park that is providing a fairly bland, gloomy and wintery feel ahead of this lunchtime WSL clash, but both teams arrive here in positive moods after good midweek victories in the League Cup.

The splash of purple – used by the hosts to redecorate some of this famous old ground’s exterior – offers a bit of colour amid the grey scenes, but otherwise the surroundings are familiar for veteran Everton fans. I’ve just spoken to a few home supporters who say they enjoy coming here for the nostalgia. They would also love a win, which would propel them up to fourth in the table.

If you want to follow the buildup to Chelsea v Man Utd, there is a dedicated live blog with Scott Murray.

Interesting news in the Chelsea lineup too as Estêvão starts. Here are the starting XIs in full …

Chelsea (3-4-3) Penders; Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill; Neto, Caicedo, Lavia, Palestra; Estêvão, Palmer, Rogers. Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Subuloye, Chavarría, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Quenda, Welbeck, Emegha.

Man Utd (4-2-3-1): Lammens; Yoro, Maguire, Martínez, Dalot; Santos, Baleba; Amad, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo. Subs: Darlow, De Ligt, Heaven, Mazraoui, Mainoo, Mount, Tielemans, Lacey, Zirkzee.

Bruno Fernandes has been named in Michael Carrick’s starting lineup to face Chelsea this lunchtime and will wear the armband. Fernandes held clear-the-air talks with Carrick this week after he was dropped to the bench for the defeat to Bournemouth last Sunday following comments about the manager’s tactics in the loss to Como.

Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane returns to action today in Der Klassiker, which is a 5.30pm (GMT) kick-off at the Allianz Arena. His record against Borussia Dortmund is, well, quite good – six goals in six Bundesliga games. But you’d expect nothing less, to be honest.

“Kane was a top player in England already,” Dortmund manager Niko Kovac said this week, “but to make another step up at his age that’s sensational and shows the danger and the quality of a player like that. We won’t get this done one on one, we’ll need to do it together.”

Kane was given a guard of honour by his teammates before Wednesday’s DFB Pokal game against Magdeburg, which he sat out on the bench.

Kane’s compatriot Aaron Danks will take charge of Bayern Munich for the second weekend in a row with Vincent Kompany still absent. Bayern said on Wednesday that Kompany had been discharged from hospital after he was admitted last week after collapsing in training. Kompany is continuing to recover at home after a meningeal infection.

“No big changes, no big differences for us. We will be ready and super competitive,” Danks said of Bayern’s approach to Der Klassiker. “There is a difference (in coaching). Vinnie did not want his assistant coaches to be mini-Vinnies. We ‌are all different but we complement each other.”

Ever wanted to ask Charlie Nicholas a question? Well, this is your chance. Whether you want to know about the season he scored 50 goals for Celtic, or the day he scored both goals as Arsenal beat Liverpool in the League Cup final, or his time on Soccer Saturday, let us know.

I’d certainly like to ask him about that Specsavers comeback at Jeff Stelling on Soccer Saturday …

Another fantastic 3pm game in prospect, and it's now dark enough for floodlights at that time. Quite right too, as football is better in the dark and drizzle, and that's a fact.

I'm especially looking forward to seeing Pascal Groß again, the best footballer with ein eszett since Thomas Häßler. Groß leads the stats this season on assists, distance covered and chances created. He's just a great playersl to watch - clever and versatile and hard working and imaginative. Can't think of any others in the league even close to his level in their mid-30s.

I don’t think it’s going overboard by saying Pascal Gross has been one of the players of the season in the Premier League so far. Also, I agree, 3pm games are just better when it gets dark at half-time.

Brighton visit the Etihad for the second time this week after losing on penalties in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. And it’s a second weekend in a row in the north-west after their trip to Anfield last Sunday. On Thursday, their travels take them to Getafe near Madrid – not as glamorous as it sounds, I’ve been there.

“Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,” Coventry’s Frank Lampard said in August. Today’s meeting at the CBS Arena is the first since the dramatic Championship playoff semi-final they contested 18 months ago – Dom Ballard and all that.

Since then, the two sides have taken diverging paths – Coventry spent another season in the second tier while Sunderland’s post-promotion form led them all the way into Europe. But today they meet as near-equals – they occupy the bottom two places in the Premier League table.

Both are in need of points and, particularly for Sunderland, in need of pride. “There’s always a new story and a new chapter to write,” Sunderland’s Regis Le Bris said this week. “This game will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars, our foundations and, after that, the game will be the game. Coventry have won twice in the Premier League so they are competitive. The Premier League is a new chapter for them but they are still efficient.”

Manchester United Women are on a roll right now. After some teething problems under new manager Eva Olid, United have won seven of their last eight games in all competitions and drew with the WSL champions in the Manchester derby last weekend.

Speaking after United’s 3-0 win over Burnley in the League Cup on Wednesday, Olid said: “This match is really good for momentum but we cannot relax on Saturday, we have Everton in the league. In the league, anything can happen and everyone is difficult to play.”

Captain Maya Le Tissier had played every minute of United’s last 118 games until she was subbed against Burnley. “She knew [about the sub], because the records are good but I need to protect her,” Olid said. “I think she needed a rest and I think it was the best decision, but still, she’s starting all games.”

Today’s game is, of course, taking place at Goodison Park, which Everton Women have to themselves after the men moved to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

It’s Wolves v Cardiff today , which is a good excuse to remember the all-time classic of April 2018. As both teams chased promotion in the Championship, Cardiff missed two stoppage-time penalties, Ruben Neves scored a great free-kick and Neil Warnock told Nuno Espirito Santo to “f*** off” for celebrating too much.

....13 games ago they also met competitively in the FA Cup semi-final (2020, Chelsea won 3-1, Covid closed doors I think) There were players of 14 different nationalities across the two starting 11s that day. Name a player and his nationality who started that game (no AI/Google cheating) - Chelsea v Man Utd FACSF 2020

Stooze does his best Alexander Armstrong impression … is Willy Caballero (Argentina) a pointless answer?

Will we see any of Estêvão at the Bridge today? Xabi Alonso has ruled out a January loan exit for the 19-year-old after questions about his limited game time. Estêvão was left on the bench for the Carabao Cup game against Liverpool and has played just 47 minutes in the Premier League so far this season.

“It’s no secret that all players want to be on the pitch,” Alonso said yesterday. “When any of them haven’t had enough minutes because of my decision, I have to take the responsibility for that. But everyone has to be ready because in any game they could be important. Este, his training and his attitude has been good.

I enjoyed Andy Hunter's article on Alexis Mac Allister this morning. The statistics he refers to were interesting and I hope Macca can keep this up.

Mac Allister’s sense of responsibility extends to implementing Iraola’s instructions for his new team. Figures from Opta show the midfielder is winning more tackles per Premier League game this season – 2.3 on average compared to 1.8 last season; winning more duels (4.8 from 3.8); winning more aerial duels (0.9 from 0.6) and winning more possession (5.6 on average compared to 3.8).

He is sacrificing the offensive side of his game to bring more aggression and organisation to the defensive aspect, and his touches in the opposition box, chances created, goals and assists are all down on last season as a consequence. Not that Iraola is complaining.

For those of you in the UK, today’s Milan derby is being shown free-to-air on BBC Two. How about that?

Inter and Milan this week unveiled plans for their new stadium that will replace San Siro from the 2031-32 season, in time for Italy to co-host Euro 2032.

The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2bn (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.

Shortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading: “You will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting: “Hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.

Premier League 12.30pm Chelsea v Man Utd 3pm Bournemouth v Leeds, Brentford v Nottingham Forest, Coventry v Sunderland, Hull v Ipswich, Man City v Brighton 5.30pm Tottenham v Crystal Palace 8pm Aston Villa v Fulham

Championship 12.30pm Lincoln v Birmingham 3pm Burnley v Portsmouth, Southampton v QPR, West Ham v West Brom

League One 12.30pm Bradford v Huddersfield, Plymouth v Reading 3pm Peterborough v Luton

It is not all rosy at Chelsea either. A home defeat to Spurs can bring any season to a grinding halt and the manner of the performance last weekend has brought Xabi Alonso under scrutiny. Wednesday’s defeat to Liverpool in the Carabao Cup has not helped, with the domestic cups surely taking higher priority this season without European football.

But perhaps the most concerning thing for Alonso is his growing injury list . In recent days and weeks he has lost Reece James, João Pedro and Maxence Lacroix – with none of them expected back for a few weeks at least. Emi Martínez could soon make a return from his broken jaw, but it will be Mike Penders in goal again today.

Here are the predicted lineups for the lunchtime clash with Manchester United …

“It’s not always rosy and nice conversations,” Michael Carrick said on Thursday as he reflected on a difficult week at United amid speculation over his future and the general state of the club.

United have gone eight games without a win after their worst league start in 40 years. They are 16th in the Premier League , one point above the relegation zone. Carrick suggested he had held talks with Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada this week …

It’s pretty clear, it’s not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that’s between me and the players, whether that’s between me, Jason, Omar or the owners.

It’s the truth, it’s the hard truth at times and it’s what we need to move forward. Whatever we need to move forward, we will do.

On the reception he was given – and the boos his players received – at Old Trafford following defeat to Bournemouth last Sunday, Carrick said …

I’ll be totally honest, it was mixed feelings for me. To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.

It wasn’t a nice situation but to feel that was important, of course, but it didn’t make me feel better in the fact that I’m with the players 100% and we’re all in it together. I’ve told the players that, I’m happy to say that.

Manchester United: What’s gone on this week? Well, you would have got long odds on Michael Carrick being in the dugout at Stamford Bridge when he trudged down the tunnel at Old Trafford last weekend.

Monday: The powers that be at Carrington – the immensely popular Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada – hold talks over Carrick’s future. Carrick attends an under-21s match at the training ground.

Tuesday: Wilcox decides to give Carrick a chance to turn things around. Bruno Fernandes holds clear-the-air talks with Carrick after sitting out the defeat to Bournemouth. Eddie Howe emerges as United’s prime candidate if Carrick is sacked.

Thursday: Carrick says he will not strip Fernandes of the captaincy and says he is not surprised to have kept his job as head coach. “Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and push things in a good direction,” Carrick says.

Should Fernandes return to the United lineup at Chelsea today? If he does, he’ll lead them out as captain.

A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being investigated by the event’s organisers, France Football, who have also contacted the police.

It has been alleged that 12 Polymarket accounts – an American cryptocurrency-based prediction market – placed the bets, with more than $264,000 wagered on the outcome before Monday’s ceremony. Their extraordinary accuracy has raised serious questions about a potential leak of confidential results before football’s most prestigious individual award.

Harry Kane was crowned the winner at the ceremony at the London Palladium, finishing ahead of Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Lionel Messi. Remarkably, this was the exact order predicted by the group of accounts identified in French media outlet Upside’s investigation.

Aston Villa have announced plans to take legal action against Jamie Carragher following his “unacceptable insults” about the club and its supporters.
