There’s a thick layer of low-hanging cloud over Goodison Park that is providing a fairly bland, gloomy and wintery feel ahead of this lunchtime WSL clash, but both teams arrive here in positive moods after good midweek victories in the League Cup.

The splash of purple – used by the hosts to redecorate some of this famous old ground’s exterior – offers a bit of colour amid the grey scenes, but otherwise the surroundings are familiar for veteran Everton fans. I’ve just spoken to a few home supporters who say they enjoy coming here for the nostalgia. They would also love a win, which would propel them up to fourth in the table.
If you want to follow the buildup to Chelsea v Man Utd, there is a dedicated live blog with Scott Murray.
Interesting news in the Chelsea lineup too as Estêvão starts. Here are the starting XIs in full …

Bruno Fernandes has been named in Michael Carrick’s starting lineup to face Chelsea this lunchtime and will wear the armband. Fernandes held clear-the-air talks with Carrick this week after he was dropped to the bench for the defeat to Bournemouth last Sunday following comments about the manager’s tactics in the loss to Como.

Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane returns to action today in Der Klassiker, which is a 5.30pm (GMT) kick-off at the Allianz Arena. His record against Borussia Dortmund is, well, quite good – six goals in six Bundesliga games. But you’d expect nothing less, to be honest.

“Kane was a top player in England already,” Dortmund manager Niko Kovac said this week, “but to make another step up at his age that’s sensational and shows the danger and the quality of a player like that. We won’t get this done one on one, we’ll need to do it together.”
Kane was given a guard of honour by his teammates before Wednesday’s DFB Pokal game against Magdeburg, which he sat out on the bench.

Kane’s compatriot Aaron Danks will take charge of Bayern Munich for the second weekend in a row with Vincent Kompany still absent. Bayern said on Wednesday that Kompany had been discharged from hospital after he was admitted last week after collapsing in training. Kompany is continuing to recover at home after a meningeal infection.

“No big changes, no big differences for us. We will be ready and super competitive,” Danks said of Bayern’s approach to Der Klassiker. “There is a difference (in coaching). Vinnie did not want his assistant coaches to be mini-Vinnies. We ‌are all different but we complement each other.”

Ever wanted to ask Charlie Nicholas a question? Well, this is your chance. Whether you want to know about the season he scored 50 goals for Celtic, or the day he scored both goals as Arsenal beat Liverpool in the League Cup final, or his time on Soccer Saturday, let us know.
I’d certainly like to ask him about that Specsavers comeback at Jeff Stelling on Soccer Saturday …
Another fantastic 3pm game in prospect, and it's now dark enough for floodlights at that time. Quite right too, as football is better in the dark and drizzle, and that's a fact.

I'm especially looking forward to seeing Pascal Groß again, the best footballer with ein eszett since Thomas Häßler. Groß leads the stats this season on assists, distance covered and chances created. He's just a great playersl to watch - clever and versatile and hard working and imaginative. Can't think of any others in the league even close to his level in their mid-30s.

I don’t think it’s going overboard by saying Pascal Gross has been one of the players of the season in the Premier League so far. Also, I agree, 3pm games are just better when it gets dark at half-time.

Brighton visit the Etihad for the second time this week after losing on penalties in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. And it’s a second weekend in a row in the north-west after their trip to Anfield last Sunday. On Thursday, their travels take them to Getafe near Madrid – not as glamorous as it sounds, I’ve been there.

“Sunderland’s story is important and something we’ve analysed,” Coventry’s Frank Lampard said in August. Today’s meeting at the CBS Arena is the first since the dramatic Championship playoff semi-final they contested 18 months ago – Dom Ballard and all that.

Since then, the two sides have taken diverging paths – Coventry spent another season in the second tier while Sunderland’s post-promotion form led them all the way into Europe. But today they meet as near-equals – they occupy the bottom two places in the Premier League table.

Both are in need of points and, particularly for Sunderland, in need of pride. “There’s always a new story and a new chapter to write,” Sunderland’s Regis Le Bris said this week. “This game will be an exciting one with our intention to be us, show up with our identity, our pillars, our foundations and, after that, the game will be the game. Coventry have won twice in the Premier League so they are competitive. The Premier League is a new chapter for them but they are still efficient.”

Manchester United Women are on a roll right now. After some teething problems under new manager Eva Olid, United have won seven of their last eight games in all competitions and drew with the WSL champions in the Manchester derby last weekend.

Speaking after United’s 3-0 win over Burnley in the League Cup on Wednesday, Olid said: “This match is really good for momentum but we cannot relax on Saturday, we have Everton in the league. In the league, anything can happen and everyone is difficult to play.”

Captain Maya Le Tissier had played every minute of United’s last 118 games until she was subbed against Burnley. “She knew [about the sub], because the records are good but I need to protect her,” Olid said. “I think she needed a rest and I think it was the best decision, but still, she’s starting all games.”
Today’s game is, of course, taking place at Goodison Park, which Everton Women have to themselves after the men moved to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

It’s Wolves v Cardiff today , which is a good excuse to remember the all-time classic of April 2018. As both teams chased promotion in the Championship, Cardiff missed two stoppage-time penalties, Ruben Neves scored a great free-kick and Neil Warnock told Nuno Espirito Santo to “f*** off” for celebrating too much.

Stooze does his best Alexander Armstrong impression … is Willy Caballero (Argentina) a pointless answer?

Will we see any of Estêvão at the Bridge today? Xabi Alonso has ruled out a January loan exit for the 19-year-old after questions about his limited game time. Estêvão was left on the bench for the Carabao Cup game against Liverpool and has played just 47 minutes in the Premier League so far this season.

“It’s no secret that all players want to be on the pitch,” Alonso said yesterday. “When any of them haven’t had enough minutes because of my decision, I have to take the responsibility for that. But everyone has to be ready because in any game they could be important. Este, his training and his attitude has been good.
I enjoyed Andy Hunter's article on Alexis Mac Allister this morning. The statistics he refers to were interesting and I hope Macca can keep this up.

Mac Allister’s sense of responsibility extends to implementing Iraola’s instructions for his new team. Figures from Opta show the midfielder is winning more tackles per Premier League game this season – 2.3 on average compared to 1.8 last season; winning more duels (4.8 from 3.8); winning more aerial duels (0.9 from 0.6) and winning more possession (5.6 on average compared to 3.8).

He is sacrificing the offensive side of his game to bring more aggression and organisation to the defensive aspect, and his touches in the opposition box, chances created, goals and assists are all down on last season as a consequence. Not that Iraola is complaining.
For those of you in the UK, today’s Milan derby is being shown free-to-air on BBC Two. How about that?
Inter and Milan this week unveiled plans for their new stadium that will replace San Siro from the 2031-32 season, in time for Italy to co-host Euro 2032.

The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2bn (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.

Shortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading: “You will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting: “Hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.

Wednesday’s defeat to Liverpool in the Carabao Cup has not helped, with the domestic cups surely taking higher priority this season without European football.

But perhaps the most concerning thing for Alonso is his growing injury list . In recent days and weeks he has lost Reece James, João Pedro and Maxence Lacroix – with none of them expected back for a few weeks at least. Emi Martínez could soon make a return from his broken jaw, but it will be Mike Penders in goal again today.

“It’s not always rosy and nice conversations,” Michael Carrick said on Thursday as he reflected on a difficult week at United amid speculation over his future and the general state of the club.

United have gone eight games without a win after their worst league start in 40 years. They are 16th in the Premier League , one point above the relegation zone. Carrick suggested he had held talks with Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada this week …
It’s pretty clear, it’s not always rosy and nice conversations between anyone, whether that’s between me and the players, whether that’s between me, Jason, Omar or the owners.
It’s the truth, it’s the hard truth at times and it’s what we need to move forward. Whatever we need to move forward, we will do.
On the reception he was given – and the boos his players received – at Old Trafford following defeat to Bournemouth last Sunday, Carrick said …
I’ll be totally honest, it was mixed feelings for me. To have the appreciation from the supporters and that connection and that respect is something I feel strongly about.

It wasn’t a nice situation but to feel that was important, of course, but it didn’t make me feel better in the fact that I’m with the players 100% and we’re all in it together. I’ve told the players that, I’m happy to say that.
Manchester United: What’s gone on this week? Well, you would have got long odds on Michael Carrick being in the dugout at Stamford Bridge when he trudged down the tunnel at Old Trafford last weekend.
Monday: The powers that be at Carrington – the immensely popular Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada – hold talks over Carrick’s future. Carrick attends an under-21s match at the training ground.

Thursday: Carrick says he will not strip Fernandes of the captaincy and says he is not surprised to have kept his job as head coach. “Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and push things in a good direction,” Carrick says.
Should Fernandes return to the United lineup at Chelsea today? If he does, he’ll lead them out as captain.

A series of suspicious bets that correctly predicted the exact top-five finishing order of this year’s Ballon d’Or and generated almost $200,000 (£149,000) in winnings is being investigated by the event’s organisers, France Football, who have also contacted the police.

It has been alleged that 12 Polymarket accounts – an American cryptocurrency-based prediction market – placed the bets, with more than $264,000 wagered on the outcome before Monday’s ceremony. articles.summary: ⚽ Updates on the 12.30pm GMT kick-off in west London ⚽ Football Daily | Goalscorers | Live Scores | Email Scott Chelsea can reclaim fourth spot with a win this afternoon. Things are possibly not quite as bad as I painted them in the preamble. Erm. But vibes are vibes, and you get the gist. Meanwhile Manchester United would feel a lot better about themselves if they make their way up to 12th, 11th or even 10th with a big win. Any such progress for the Red Devils would only be guaranteed for a couple of hours, on this eight-game Super Saturday, but baby steps. Both teams welcome back a fan favourite. Estevao starts for Chelsea, while Bruno Fernandes returns for Manchester United. Jordan Henderson is absent through illness, while Cole Palmer returns after suspension. Kobbie Mainoo is back on the United bench after a few matches out injured. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Chelsea can reclaim fourth spot with a win this afternoon. Things are possibly not quite as bad as I painted them in the preamble. Erm. But vibes are vibes, and you get the gist. Meanwhile Manchester United would feel a lot better about themselves if they make their way up to 12th, 11th or even 10th with a big win. Any such progress for the Red Devils would only be guaranteed for a couple of hours, on this eight-game Super Saturday, but baby steps.

Both teams welcome back a fan favourite. Estevao starts for Chelsea, while Bruno Fernandes returns for Manchester United . Jordan Henderson is absent through illness, while Cole Palmer returns after suspension. Kobbie Mainoo is back on the United bench after a few matches out injured.

Chelsea: Penders, Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill, Pedro Neto, Caicedo, Lavia, Palestra, Estevao, Palmer, Rogers. Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Barco, Welbeck, Emegha, Quenda, Gusto, Chavarria, Nicoll-Jazuli, Subuloye.

Manchester United: Lammens, Yoro, Martinez, Maguire, Dalot, Santos, Baleba, Diallo, Fernandes, Cunha, Mbeumo. Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, de Ligt, Mount, Zirkzee, Tielemans, Heaven, Lacey, Mainoo.

Referee: Peter Bankes The welcome return of VAR, after a week in the League Cup when nobody noticed it had gone: James Bell

None of these lads have started the season as they’d have liked. Chelsea may be fifth in the Premier League table, but they’re out of the League Cup , the fanbase aren’t yet all in on formation-fluid Xabi Alonso, and as Andrew Beasley recently reported …

… their expected-points performance has actually been worse than 16th-placed Manchester United , who are themselves in all manner of bother right now. It’s fair to say that both Alonso and Michael Carrick could do with a win this lunchtime, albeit those hopes are laced with varying degrees of desperation: a defeat would certainly turn up the heat on Alonso, but it might prove one misstep too many for Carrick, whose coat hangs heavy on the shoogliest of pegs. But then we thought that after the Bournemouth debacle last Sunday, and here we all remain. So nobody knows anything for sure … but be certain that the noises-off will get louder, far louder, for someone, somewhere, after the result of this game is in. A draw probably won’t help anyone very much either. Kick-off is at 12.30pm GMT. It’s on!

articles.title: Australia 66-6 Cook Islands: men’s Rugby League World Cup – as it happened
articles.summary: Kangaroos shake off a slow start to defeat Cook Islands in Townsville Australia cruise into the semi-finals on top of Pool A The Kangaroos will be wearing their familiar dark green uniform with gold accents. Plenty of green in the Cook Islands outfit as well, but it is the secondary colour to a majority white base. Tonight’s referee is NRL veteran Ashley Klein. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Thank you for joining me this evening. Australia are still not firing on all cylinders but they’re now just 160 minutes away from yet another World Cup triumph. I’ll see you back here next weekend for a couple of mouthwatering semi-finals. Here is Jack Snape ’s report from the Kangaroos’ 66-6 win over Cook Islands in Townsville …

Reece Walsh showed if there was anything James Tedesco could do, he can do better with a starring role for the Kangaroos in a partly clunky but otherwise entertaining victory over the Cook Islands in Townsville.

Coach Kevin Walters faces a choice between the two brilliant No 1s for the much-anticipated semi-final against either Samoa or Tonga next week, but this only sometimes convincing display showed there is still work to do in camp Kangaroo.

Although we’re technically still in the group phase we are now effectively into the knockouts.

Lebanon and France will complete their duties from 5:40pm tomorrow, after which it’s blockbusters all the way, starting with Tonga v Samoa to establish which of the Pacific Island nations will finish top of the group and play New Zealand, and which will finish second and take on Australia.

Then it’s onto those massive semi-finals next weekend, before the decider in Brisbane on Sunday 15th November.

The Kangaroos are still well short of their best. We have yet to see Origin-level intensity and discipline.

Player of the match Reece Walsh is in the box seat to wear the No 1 jersey next weekend. His ability to drift into the line on either edge and open the game as a second playmaker is so fun to watch.

Tom Dearden should start in the No 7 jersey after a decent outing, but he could yet be overtaken by Sam Walker purely for the Roosters’ goal-kicking ability. Walsh started the night as the designated kicker but was hampered by a foot injury that forced Munster then Strange to take over conversion duties.

The forward pack remains a work in progress. Yeo, Carrigan, Martin, and Grant all made uncharacteristic errors in possession, but there was also plenty of dynamic running, from Preston and Fa’asuamaleaui in particular.

Ethan Strange has forced his way into contention for a spot on the bench. His versatility and effervescence make him an ideal man to have among the six reserves and he added plenty of impetus in the second half.

The hosts and defending champions win Pool A and make it safely through to the semi-finals.

Chaos in Townsville. Australia should score in the right corner after a brilliant pass from Walsh. Then Cook Islands should run the ball clear after an interception but spill the ball on the ground. The Kangaroos come back at speed and Walsh sends the whole of the stadium to the left before passing to Grant on his right hip to send the hooker behind the posts.

76 mins: Cook Islands continue to give their all in the dying stages. Takairangi in particular has left it all out there.

74 mins: Now Takairangi drops the pass at first receiver on the last. Someone put a fork in this one, it is done.

72 mins: Carrigan with the loose carry just after returning to the fray off the bench.

70 mins: Marsters is enjoying a golden spell on the ball. Takairangi kicks early in the set – there’s room behind, the sprint is on – but the ball beats Rennie and Bostock and bobbles out of play.

68 mins: Cook Islands have a second wind! They regather the dropout then Teague almost hustles his way through. Ngatikaura tries to repeat his snipe from dummy-half that worked so well early on. The on the last, under the crossbar, Fa’asuamaleaui concedes a brainless penalty, and the siege continues.

67 mins: And they force a dropout! Marsters gets busy, Takairangi dabs a kick over the top, and Bostock is forced to take the conservative option.

66 mins: A rare spell of Cook Islands possession after Staggs is scragged and dragged into touch.

64 mins: Strange has made a difference coming off the bench. He’s brought urgency and intensity into the game and his effervescent has rubbed off on Munster who has played with more characteristic freedom since half-time.

62 mins: Australia think they’ve scored again but Walsh is instead pinged for a forward pass, tipping on what looked to the naked eye like a majestic try-assist to Staggs. To add injury to insult the fullback reels away in pain after taking a heavy hit from Holmes. Walsh’s kicking foot, his left, is far from 100%.

Aaaaaand another. Walsh again too quick and strong carving through the line on the left edge. He could assist on his inside to Best but chooses Bostock on his outside instead and it’s hat-tricks all round for Australia’s wingers.

Trbojevic has another Temu hat-trick. The Cooks Islands’ defence is done for the night and Walsh on the burst is way too quick and powerful to stop. He hares towards the left corner but before attempting to score himself feeds an inside pass to Trbojevic who almost fluffs his moment just inches from the line with KL Iro executing a fierce tackle but the big winger manages to plant the ball down.

Two six-agains in the restart set as the Kangaroos cruise deep inside Cook Islands territory. Then Tino Fa’asuamaleaui spots a gap, executes a sidestep, pins his ears back and tears towards the line for a fourth try in quick succession.

42 mins: Simple from the Kangaroos first-up with a set punctuated by a Grant snipe that allows Dearden to gain metres on the right edge. Brown then continues his horror night by losing the ball in contact and Australia have a full set inside the red zone.

Reece Walsh has done well at fullback but he looks to be carrying a knock.

Jacob Preston has made two eye-catching try-assist linebreaks on the left edge.

There are still plenty of issues to solve for Kevin Walters though. Against modest opposition the Kangaroos have completed at just 66%, conceded seven errors, and executed only one offload. All world cup so far Australia have played with a lack of intensity and focus. It’s understandable tonight in a virtual dead rubber but the lack of leadership and attitude in green is concerning.

Feel free to spend your half-time break following the cricket. It has been South Africa’s morning so far as the third Test and the series goes down to the wire.

Australia are comfortably the superior of the two sides but there are still serious issues with execution for the defending champions.

There are numbers on the right but a combinatino of inaccurate passing and Australia’s desperation denies the score. Cook Islands come again and Takairangi grubbers through on tackle two but the Kangaroos are well set. The underdogs get the ball back again and this time Holmes tries to grubber on the left, but to no avail.

37 mins: Another sloppy couple of phases from the Kangaroos. First up there’s a poor connection on the left edge with a try in the offing following the penalty to Munster. Then Yeo loses his bearings on halfway and instead of accepting contact throws a pass that’s both forward and off target.

35 mins: Ooof! A massive sharp intake of breath as Munster yelps in pain as Holmes near-hip-drop tackles the stand-off as he took bodies with him towards the posts. He seems ok, thankfully. Meanwhile replays show Trbojevic wincing after rolling his ankle. Kevin Walters will be keeping Ethan Strange on his toes.

Too easy for the Kangaroos. On defensive 30 Australia shift from the right edge through hands to Munster who holds the ball up and drops it inside to Preston who accelerates through a non-existent defensive line. For the second time tonight the Bulldog has only one man to beat and this time he draws in Holmes then offloads to Walsh on his shoulder. A training ground 70m score.

articles.title: ‘A gust of wind blowing back her hair added something special’: Mark McEvoy’s best phone picture
articles.summary: It was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist? This Margate shop is now an ice-cream parlour, but back in 2014 it was a vintage clothes store. Mark McEvoy, who had relocated from London the previous year with his partner and baby daughter, approached the young woman to ask permission to take this shot. “I remember it being a very cold October day, so I was surprised she was barelegged and barefoot,” he says. “My guess is that she was working in the shop, or maybe a friend of someone working there. The fur coat may even have been for sale inside, just something she put on to keep warm during a cigarette break.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
It was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist?

T his Margate shop is now an ice-cream parlour, but back in 2014 it was a vintage clothes store. Mark McEvoy, who had relocated from London the previous year with his partner and baby daughter, approached the young woman to ask permission to take this shot.

“I remember it being a very cold October day, so I was surprised she was barelegged and barefoot,” he says. “My guess is that she was working in the shop, or maybe a friend of someone working there. The fur coat may even have been for sale inside, just something she put on to keep warm during a cigarette break.”

McEvoy didn’t notice the blond-haired, barelegged mannequin in the window until he stepped back. “A gust of wind blowing back her hair and her pose added something special,” he notes.

In more recent years, McEvoy has been scanning and collating his 40-year archive of photographs, and reflecting on his work across various devices and formats; a range of iPhone models but also analogue cameras, both 35mm and medium format. “I am a bit of a purist, inspired by the documentary tradition of cropping in the frame when you take the photo. So, rather than say to myself, ‘I can crop that out in post’, I’ll move physically closer to the subject instead,” McEvoy says.

It’s an approach he would recommend to any aspiring photographer. “These days, with AI and advanced editing software, it’s too easy to manipulate a photo, and the line between fact and fiction becomes more and more blurred.”

articles.title: Fallon Sherrock pulls off shock defeat of world darts No 1 Luke Littler in live TV battle
articles.summary: The 15th amateur to challenge Littler in Netflix stream on Friday evening, Sherrock was ‘lost for words’ after winning £501,000 prize The name of the programme was Beat Luke Littler, and Fallon Sherrock did just that. On one of the biggest nights of the year for British TV, Netflix, too, there was much at stake: not just £501,000 to any of the 20 amateur challengers who managed to beat Littler in a single leg of darts, but also the jeopardy of whether audiences would choose to watch the streamer’s first UK live entertainment event – or the final of BBC juggernaut The Celebrity Traitors. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The 15th amateur to challenge Littler in Netflix stream on Friday evening, Sherrock was ‘lost for words’ after winning £501,000 prize

The name of the programme was Beat Luke Littler, and Fallon Sherrock did just that.

On one of the biggest nights of the year for British TV, Netflix , too, there was much at stake: not just £501,000 to any of the 20 amateur challengers who managed to beat Littler in a single leg of darts, but also the jeopardy of whether audiences would choose to watch the streamer’s first UK live entertainment event – or the final of BBC juggernaut The Celebrity Traitors.

Netflix also had no idea when or whether the world champion would be beaten at the packed event at Manchester Central arena, hosted by Gary Lineker and Richard Osman, so had put in place contingency plans to have a second place competition should Littler lose within the first few rounds.

However, watched by hundreds of his fans, “the Nuke” comfortably beat a range of contestants of differing abilities who had queued up to take part in heats during the summer, including 14-year-olds Mackinley Cooper-Johnson and Jayden Walker.

Cheered on by enthusiastic crowds in fancy dress, one contender came close to claiming the lucrative prize, the former Irish youth darts player Pearse Mackle. But in the end it took about two-and-a-half hours for Littler to lose, to the 15th contender, Sherrock.

There was some controversy when it was revealed she was competing earlier this month: after all, she has an MBE for services to darts, and some people claimed she was not a true amateur, having played at the PDC World Darts Championship and won the inaugural Women’s World Matchplay in 2022. But Netflix classed anyone who has not ever had a PDC tour card as being eligible to take part.

“I mean, it’s been tough,” Sherrock said after her victory in Manchester. “Obviously I do see the backlash and I do see all the negative comments. But at the end of the day, I fit the criteria for this. I’ve never had a tour card, and I wouldn’t class myself as a pro really, because all I do is just play darts for the enjoyment of it.”

The PDC president, Barry Hearn, who was involved in the audition process, defended the contest. Asked whether Sherrock’s inclusion was unfair, Hearn said: “No, not at all. She’s not a PDC tour card holder. She’s entitled to enter. Why should she be denied?”

Despite her experience it was still a shock to the crowd that Sherrock defeated Littler. “I can’t put into words how much this means,” she told Lineker after her win, which was greeted by huge cheers from the delighted audience and a hug from her young son. “I’m really lost for words right now. It was a great moment. Give me an opportunity and I’ll take it every time … I’m really proud of myself.”

Littler, a magnanimous loser, said Sherrock had been “world class. I’ve enjoyed every bit of it … everything leading up to this. Maybe Netflix we can do it again next year.”

Beat Luke Littler was undoubtedly a risk for Netflix but it looks to have paid off as sources said audience numbers stayed steady (they could vote for the order the players appeared in) despite the competition from The Celebrity Traitors, and appeared to rise after the end of the BBC show.

The show, dreamed up by the Manchester-based production company Workerbee, brings more working-class audiences to the streamer and helps its drive to air more live mainstream events. It echoes similar events in other sports pitting ordinary people against the elite, such as the Million Dollar 1 Point Slam at the Australian Open tennis tournament.

Workerbee’s managing director, Michelle Chappell, told the Guardian: “Rick Murray, our CEO, came up with the idea, which was just: ‘Wouldn’t it be amazing if someone could take on Luke Littler.’ It’s a sport event but a big show at the same time and it’s got a sense of humour and real jeopardy.”

There was one winner guaranteed, though, in the battle between Beat Luke Littler and The Celebrity Traitors, and that was the global production company Banijay – which owns the companies that make the two shows.

articles.content:
The actor on his ill-fated music career, a rumoured love child, and the project driving him up the wall

B orn in Stockport, Greater Manchester, Will Mellor, 50, joined Brookside at 16 and was cast as Jambo in Hollyoaks in 1995. He appeared in Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps, Line of Duty, and was a regular in Coronation Street from 2021. His recent dramas are Mr Bates vs the Post Office and A Woman of Substance; his factual programmes include Convictions Gone Bad. On 5 November his memoir, Where There’s a Will: My Story , is published. He is married with two children and lives in Buckinghamshire.

What do you most dislike about your appearance? My bent nose and my ears. They don’t stop growing, so I’ve got a big nose and big ears.

If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose? I’d like to see my dad again, just to hug him. It was Covid when he passed away and I never got to say goodbye.

What is your most unappealing habit? Picking my nose. I can’t help it because it’s bent and I get stuff stuck up there.

Which book are you ashamed not to have read? I don’t really read books, so all of them.

What is the worst thing anyone’s said to you? When I was doing music, somebody came up to me and said, “You’ve changed.” It was the worst thing and the best thing – because I left the record industry. It was not for me and I’d become somebody I didn’t like.

Would you choose fame or anonymity? I’ve been an attention-seeker since I was a kid, so I’d choose fame.

What or who is the greatest love of your life? My wife, Michelle. I’ve been with her for 27 years. We’re a great team and have two amazing children.

Which phrase do you most overuse? “You can’t make an omelette without breaking eggs.” I keep thinking it because I’ve been having my house renovated for the past six months and it’s driving me up the wall.

What has been your biggest disappointment? I would have liked to have made the Strictly final [he got to the semi-final].

If you could edit your past, what would you change? There was a lady who made out that she’d had my child, so the girl went to school telling people that her dad was on TV. When we did the DNA test, she found out she wasn’t mine. I feel sorry for her because she’d been lied to, and I wish I could change that.

What do you consider your greatest achievement? Having a stable family.

What has been your closest brush with the law? Because my dad was in prison when I was a kid, he made sure that wasn’t a place that I was ever going to go. He was a bit of a Del Boy – so dodgy MOTs, stolen stuff. He went to Strangeways for almost a year and left me and my mum and my four sisters unprotected, and he hated every second.

articles.summary: Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll In his heyday, Larry Johnson was the NFL tailback you’d least want to line up against, the steamroller in pads who had defensive players and coaches questioning their life choices on every down. articles.content:
Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll

I n his heyday, Larry Johnson was the NFL tailback you’d least want to line up against, the steamroller in pads who had defensive players and coaches questioning their life choices on every down. But since Johnson walked away from pro football in 2011, after seven seasons in the league and an All-Pro run with the Kansas City Chiefs , he’s the one doing the soul-searching, grappling with the toll all that gridiron glory has taken on his brain.

Johnson, who still cuts a fit and formidable figure at age 46, can scarcely recall his glittering career, much less its highlights. “I go up to maybe 2006, 2007,” he tells me. “Anything before or three years after, I really don’t remember.”

When Johnson was thriving as a pro in the mid 2000s, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, was not yet widely recognized as a risk of playing football. The NFL, however, had evidence that head injuries could cause lasting neurological damage, yet spent much of the decade publicly disputing the link as former players sought disability benefits for neurological problems – and were largely denied.

It wasn’t until Will Smith starred in the movie Concussion as Bennett Omalu – the forensic pathologist who sounded the alarm on CTE in American football players after examining the brain of Mike Webster, the Hall of Fame center who died in 2002 after years of cognitive decline and a range of behavioral problems – that Johnson began joining the dots between football and his own personality swings. Johnson has long suspected he suffers from CTE, even though the disease can only be diagnosed after death. A study published on Wednesday of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE. Of the nearly 400 players whose brains were donated for postmortem examination, 93.5% showed evidence of the disease.

Johnson’s NFL career was defined by physical punishment, and he was a violent runner who welcomed the blows. Ahead of the 2003 draft, Johnson seemed like everything a team could want in a franchise running back. He had size (6ft 1in, 230 lbs) and speed (4.45s 40-yard dash). He capped a four-year career at Penn State by sweeping the Doak Walker Award for the nation’s best running back and the Maxwell and Walter Camp awards for the nation’s best player after rushing for more than 2,000 yards on fewer carries than anyone in history. He had backing from Joe Paterno, when that still meant something , and more hands-on guidance from his father, Larry Johnson Sr – the former Nittany Lions defensive assistant who’s now Ohio State’s associate head coach.

But when the Chiefs selected Johnson 27th overall as insurance for franchise running back Priest Holmes, they did so over the objections of head coach Dick Vermeil, who had watched a parade of Penn State runners disappoint in the pros and figured Johnson would be no different. Vermeil singled out Johnson’s preparation habits and maturity, joking that he needed to “ take the diapers off ”. But Vermeil had to eat his words after Holmes went down with a season-ending neck injury midway through the 2005 season and Johnson stepped in to rack up 1,750 yards and 20 touchdowns in nine weeks. (“Well, he’s a talent,” the coach conceded later.)

The following season Vermeil retired and Herm Edwards took over, and the bombastic defensive guru made Johnson the centerpiece of the Chiefs offense. He ran for 1,789 yards on a whopping 416 carries – an NFL record that isn’t likely to be threatened in the current era of pass-happy offense and running by committee. Whenever Johnson publicly shares his CTE fears, fans often find themselves looking back at the season for answers. Was that the beginning? Too many blows? “People forget: I didn’t get hurt during those 416 carries,” he says. “I didn’t really start until 2006. I was in the league for three years – maybe the only first-round pick battling just to dress . If Herm had told me straight up, ‘I’m gonna run you 416 times.’ I would’ve been like, Why can’t we do 500?”

Johnson reveled in his star status, famously signing on as an ambassador for Jay-Z’s Roc-A-Fella record label as it was growing into a lifestyle brand. The Chiefs workhorse was frequently spotted partying with LeBron James and other members of Jay-Z’s inner circle at the rapper mogul’s bygone 40/40 Club in New York, helping get Jay-Z in the door with the NFL and paving the way for his later relationship with the league office and commissioner Roger Goodell. Johnson celebrated touchdowns by tenting his hands into a diamond , a gesture popularized by Jay-Z and his associates known as “throwing up the Roc”.

But the southern Maryland native never quite cottoned to the scrutiny that came with the spotlight. He was slammed in the press for demanding a trade and threatening to sit out as leverage for a new contract. He clashed with Chiefs coach Todd Haley – questioning his credentials to succeed Edwards – and disparaged fans and media with homophobic slurs, prompting suspensions before he was eventually released by the team.

Johnson drew more troubling headlines for his alleged assaults on women: a Kansas City nightclub patron accused him of spitting a drink in her face , and an ex-girlfriend accused him of beating and strangling her at the Bellagio in Las Vegas. Between 2003 and 2012, he was arrested five times in cases involving allegations of violence against women – resulting in convictions for disturbing the peace, domestic battery and assault, with penalties that stopped short of jail time. Johnson shies from blaming football for those incidents, but it’s hard not to wonder what the game left behind in a man so handsomely rewarded for violence – or how much the game messed with his head. Johnson began playing tackle football at age nine, taking helmet-to-helmet hits long before he reached the NFL.

Life after football was deeply unsettling for Johnson. “I couldn’t find anything that really will test your manhood and also test your character like football,” he says. “I enjoyed lining up eight in a box and then trying to get five or 10 yards – and then I’m getting 50. As twisted as it may sound, the thing I wanted to do was to die on the football field. I always felt like I had to go to war, like I had to fight even when I don’t have to fight.”

He had hoped to transition into nonprofit work, but found the 9-to-5 office environment stifling. A hair-trigger sensitivity to light, noise and group settings made it impossible for him to hold down a job. He fought with the mother of his young daughter, Jaylen, over school pickup schedules; during a two-year court fight, with Johnson’s own mother acting as a go-between, he finally realized he was the one misremembering the times. He enrolled in a master’s program with a cohort of NFL retirees, but says he quit after flipping out on a professor during a group project.

All the while, Johnson wrestled with intrusive thoughts and inner voices telling him to harm himself and others. The voices come in waves, he says, “almost like a suggestion. Certain things scare me. I can’t be close to balconies anymore. If I’m walking, I’ll think, What if something falls out of the sky ? Just a constant state of paranoia.” To cope, he isolated himself for long stretches and self-medicated with drugs and alcohol – making matters far worse.

Johnson’s father had little idea of his son’s quiet suffering until the ex-Chiefs star went public in a 2017 Washington Post profile . Johnson feared that his father might not understand or relate to what he was going through; he went from checking in with his dad for any reason, even if it was just to say he was heading home after a game, to pulling away from his great mentor. The Post article, though, “gave my father new eyes,” Johnson says. “People would tell him, ‘That’s a really good thing your son did.’ I think that made him a little bit more accepting. [Now] we’re back to our relationship – as if I’m still in the house, you know?”

Johnson had another major breakthrough around the same time, when the NFL granted him lifetime disability benefits, giving him the financial security to focus on his health without worrying about making ends meet. In a league infamous for publicly denying former players’ claims and using race-norming to limit disability payouts (disputes that were ostensibly addressed in a revised league settlement ), that victory shouldn’t be taken lightly. Johnson knows how fortunate he was to last seven years in a league where the average running back’s career is around 2½ years, leaving little time to build a safety net. He believes the modern trend of devaluing running backs only serves a league that’s “trying to lessen payments.”

Johnson’s daily life is still punctuated by bouts of confusion. Light and noise still bother him, and he gets irritated anytime he hears himself slurring words or otherwise struggling to put sentences together. But Johnson has better ways of coping. Jaylen is old enough to drive herself – and her dad – around now, sparing him the embarrassment of getting lost on routine trips or confusing the TV remote for a car key fob . Johnson spends a lot of time talking through his feelings with his wife, who knows when to prod and when to leave him be. All of it helps keep the voices at bay, but he still hears them. He likens the intrusive thoughts to a movie. “Yours might last for a scene,” he says. “Mine is like a sequel. Then there’s part three and hidden features. It’s like Marvel at the end of the movie. It engulfs me.”

Social media tends to be where Johnson gets in trouble these days, courting controversy with conspiracy theories about Jews, Kobe Bryant’s death and Jay-Z, with whom he has since fallen out. Away from the online fray, though, Johnson keeps a cool head in group chats with former teammates, even as it frustrates him that his peers never want to talk about what they’re really going through. “All they’re talking about is each other’s birthdays and going out and drinking,” he says. “We are in an era where if you admit you were hurt, you’re soft – you know what I mean?”

His new dream is to create an app that connects former pros struggling with their mental health with people who understand what they’re going through – former NFL clinicians like Susan Wilson, his team therapist at the Chiefs. “I would love to be able to have a symposium for retired guys,” Johnson says, “so they can hear not only the horror stories, but share their similar histories of how to deal with mental health. It’s been too hush-hush and taboo for such a long time because guys are embarrassed.”

CTE researchers are always keen to build relationships with former players, too. Last month, Emory University announced a partnership with the Concussion & CTE Foundation and Boston University on a medical study of former football players experiencing depressive and cognitive symptoms. The study is testing whether an FDA-approved drug that reduces inflammation can also improve those symptoms, recruiting men aged 30–55 in the Atlanta area who have played at least 11 years of tackle football.

Whether researchers are any closer to diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients remains an open question. “CTE is both a complex physiological and psychological issue,” says Concussion & CTE Foundation co-founder Chris Nowinski, a longtime advocate . “Learning you have CTE can have a positive mental impact for some, and a negative one for others. That’s why it’s critical to have a multi-pronged approach advancing diagnosis, treatment and mental health support.”

Johnson tries not to let his emotions get the better of him when watching football now. He appreciates the safety measures the league has introduced to protect players, but laments what they’ve taken away from the physical brand of football he once defined. It broke the ex-Chief’s heart to see his former AFC rival Chris Johnson opening up about his ALS battle . “To watch these players who could basically run 4.5, 4.4 40s be in wheelchairs, like, that haunts me,” he says. “If this could happen to Chris Johnson or Steve Gleason , it can happen to any of us, right?”

In an effort to keep tabs on his own neurological condition, Johnson has taken to posting videos of himself on social media and scrutinizing them for signs of decline – the ultimate mental health self-scout. Early replies describing his delivery as “mean” or “condescending” helped him modulate his behavior and even led to some online friendships. With a firmer handle on his general well-being, Johnson thinks differently about being tested for CTE now, while he’s alive.

“When I first said that, it was like, yeah, I would want to know,” he says. “But at the end of the day, I know I would obsess over it. I would be paying attention to every little micro movement and emotion. I would drive myself crazy thinking I don’t have much time, so let me act out. If there was a way we could figure out before then, at least I would know the damage. Whether I know it or whether I can feel it, I know something is there.”

CTE researchers are always keen to build relationships with former players, too. Last month, Emory University announced a partnership with the Concussion & CTE Foundation and Boston University on a medical study of former football players experiencing depressive and cognitive symptoms. The study is testing whether an FDA-approved drug that reduces inflammation can also improve those symptoms, recruiting men aged 30–55 in the Atlanta area who have played at least 11 years of tackle football.

Whether researchers are any closer to diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients remains an open question. “CTE is both a complex physiological and psychological issue,” says Concussion & CTE Foundation co-founder Chris Nowinski, a longtime advocate . “Learning you have CTE can have a positive mental impact for some, and a negative one for others. That’s why it’s critical to have a multi-pronged approach advancing diagnosis, treatment and mental health support.”

Johnson tries not to let his emotions get the better of him when watching football now. He appreciates the safety measures the league has introduced to protect players, but laments what they’ve taken away from the physical brand of football he once defined. It broke the ex-Chief’s heart to see his former AFC rival Chris Johnson opening up about his ALS battle . “To watch these players who could basically run 4.5, 4.4 40s be in wheelchairs, like, that haunts me,” he says. “If this could happen to Chris Johnson or Steve Gleason , it can happen to any of us, right?”

In an effort to keep tabs on his own neurological condition, Johnson has taken to posting videos of himself on social media and scrutinizing them for signs of decline – the ultimate mental health self-scout. Early replies describing his delivery as “mean” or “condescending” helped him modulate his behavior and even led to some online friendships. With a firmer handle on his general well-being, Johnson thinks differently about being tested for CTE now, while he’s alive.

“When I first said that, it was like, yeah, I would want to know,” he says. “But at the end of the day, I know I would obsess over it. I would be paying attention to every little micro movement and emotion. I would drive myself crazy thinking I don’t have much time, so let me act out. If there was a way we could figure out before then, at least I would know the damage. Whether I know it or whether I can feel it, I know something is there.”

articles.title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game
articles.summary: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa “We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game. “Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa

“We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.

“Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”

The Guardian joined the pair in a Newcastle front room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.

If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.

Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.

“We were at a house party with a mutual friend and I was singing James Blunt’s Wisemen in one of the bedrooms, quite drunk,” said Purcell. “Andy happened to pass by the bedroom door, heard me singing and decided to join in. So we became fast friends from there.”

Their shared love of Dungeons & Dragons and phases playing Yu-Gi-Oh!, a trading card game, and Carcassonne, a board game, have kept the friendship going. When another friend mentioned The Campaign For North Africa, a 1979 game designed by Richard Berg simulating the desert war of 1940-43, they set out to discover more.

They watched a few videos, read up about it and went to the pub. “We both realised that we’d been thinking about the game for two weeks. By the end of the night, we were committed to giving it a try,” said Purcell.

Along with buying the game – £970 from eBay – they decided to chronicle their journey on a weekly podcast, War With a Mate . “We knew there was no reason to keep playing unless we’re held accountable,” said Purcell. “Otherwise we knew we’d buy the game, we’d give up inside two weeks and we’d have a thousand-pound board game that we can do nothing with.

“With a podcast, people can follow along and if we back out we’ve got the shame of everyone calling us out on it.”

The pair have spent 99 podcast episodes chronicling their prep and practice for the game before starting it at 7.30pm on Friday for episode 100. It could take 20 years, but “originally it was looking like 50,” said Purcell, not wanting to contemplate the idea of still playing as they approached 80.

On Friday afternoon, they were setting up in a friend’s house because they will livestream day one. It will normally be played at Taeger’s flat.

The game comes with a 10ft map, which they have divided up into five picture frames and 1,600 pieces, which they will magnetise. “We haven’t punched the German pieces out yet because we won’t need them for about five years,” said Purcell.

They will have to keep track of aircraft, truck convoys, land units, supply dumps, water use, fuel evaporation and so, so much more, including not to do anything that could be deemed a war crime.

It comes with a history book as well as seven rule books with a dizzying list. One of the best known is the “pasta rule” about Italian forces needing more water in order to boil their pasta rations. It’s assumed to be a joke – but who knows?

Berg does seem to be “poking fun” at the players, said Purcell. At the same time, he clearly also has a thorough knowledge of the campaign. “The amount of research behind this must have been insane,” said Taeger.

Purcell is playing as the Axis forces and Taeger as the Commonwealth. It remains to be seen if the game will be so historically accurate that Purcell is destined to lose. He doesn’t think so.

“I think we’ve seen already, through the practice run, you can very much change the fate of the campaign through better decision-making,” he said.

Both think the game could very well end up a draw, which would be gutting. “I think, honestly, a loss might even be better than a draw because at least it’s a definitive result,” said Taeger. There is also the chance they’ll find that the game is simply not finishable, but thanks to the podcast, they will have plenty of people cheering them on.

“The reaction has been surprisingly positive,” said Purcell, with many boardgamers thankful that someone is doing it so they don’t have to. “We’ve not really had many people decry it as the stupid thing that it is, which would be the natural reaction.”

The players are determined, but they also intend to take it seriously – and tread very carefully.

“You don’t want to make a mistake because you were in a bit of a rush,” said Taeger, definitely laughing now. “You might have to be dealing with it for the next 10 years.”

articles.title: No big deal: how Mac Allister shook off contract doubts to fire Liverpool’s revival
articles.summary: Iraola’s midfield has rediscovered its aggression and intensity just in time for Sunday’s visit of Arsenal to Anfield Alexis Mac Allister found himself in a strong position to apply pressure on Liverpool over a new contract before Atlético Madrid’s visit to Anfield last month , although only in the physical sense of being up on stage to preview the game in front of a mass audience. In reality, the 27-year-old’s negotiating stance was relatively weak. And in fairness to the Argentina international, he has been true to his word in flipping the narrative in his favour ever since. As the past two Premier League champions prepare to meet at Anfield on Sunday, when Liverpool can narrow the gap on Arsenal to three points with a fourth successive home win in all competitions, Mac Allister’s form encapsulates the impressive improvement of Andoni Iraola’s team. He has become the indispensable part of Liverpool’s central midfield and to an extent that, merely seven weeks on from that headline-grabbing Champions League press conference, it is not only Mac Allister who thinks he deserves a contract extension. articles.content:
Iraola’s midfield has rediscovered its aggression and intensity just in time for Sunday’s visit of Arsenal to Anfield

A lexis Mac Allister found himself in a strong position to apply pressure on Liverpool over a new contract before Atlético Madrid’s visit to Anfield last month , although only in the physical sense of being up on stage to preview the game in front of a mass audience. In reality, the 27-year-old’s negotiating stance was relatively weak. And in fairness to the Argentina international, he has been true to his word in flipping the narrative in his favour ever since.

As the past two Premier League champions prepare to meet at Anfield on Sunday, when Liverpool can narrow the gap on Arsenal to three points with a fourth successive home win in all competitions, Mac Allister’s form encapsulates the impressive improvement of Andoni Iraola’s team. He has become the indispensable part of Liverpool’s central midfield and to an extent that, merely seven weeks on from that headline-grabbing Champions League press conference, it is not only Mac Allister who thinks he deserves a contract extension.

“The fans don’t need to worry as I will give my 100% and maybe they [Liverpool] change their minds,” said the midfielder after expressing sadness over the absence of a new contract offer and a little envy, cloaked in happiness, over the ones awarded to Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch. The following night he struck an immaculate winner against Diego Simeone’s side. He has continued to walk the walk for a Liverpool team that has rediscovered its intensity and started to repair relations with the Anfield crowd as a result. Winning does that.

Iraola said on Friday: “You mention the press conference he had and I was there also, after him. The most important thing from that is that he wants to stay here. That is very important. He wants to work hard, he wants to be at his best so he can continue here helping us. A player of that level who has achieved what he has achieved, who can be as clear as that with his intentions, is very good for us because I appreciate him a lot. He’s a top player.”

A major influence when Liverpool won their 20th league championship under Arne Slot, Mac Allister faded badly in the Dutchman’s second and final season in charge. He was not alone on that score but, despite reminding a global audience of his qualities as Argentina reached a second World Cup final in succession, rumours of an Anfield exit this summer were met with a general shrug of shoulders rather than howls of protest. Liverpool’s stance over a contract that had entered its final two years confirmed they also didn’t consider an extension a priority. The club have also been paying Mac Allister a lucrative salary from the moment he walked through the door in June 2023, having signed him for £35m – below market value – due to a release clause in his Brighton contract.

It was largely overlooked at the time of the Atlético press conference but Mac Allister’s refusal to use a painful groin injury as an excuse for last season’s struggles reflected the character of a winner. “I don’t think that was why,” he said that day, declining the easy option. “I take responsibility because it was not a good season for me individually and for us as a team.”

The midfielder’s sense of responsibility extends to implementing Iraola’s instructions for his new team. Figures from Opta show Mac Allister is winning more tackles per Premier League game this season – 2.3 on average compared to 1.8 last season; winning more duels (4.8 from 3.8); winning more aerial duels (0.9 from 0.6) and winning more possession (5.6 on average compared to 3.8). He is sacrificing the offensive side of his game to bring more aggression and organisation to the defensive aspect, and his touches in the opposition box, chances created, goals and assists are all down on last season as a consequence. Not that Iraola is complaining.

“The thing about Mac Allister is that he understands the game overall, not just the demands of his position,” Iraola added. “It is just what is happening overall in the game. Sometimes he is the first one to correct his teammates, not just the one who is next to him. He understands what is happening around him which is a very important quality to have.”

Last season, and early in the current one as Liverpool adapted to their change of coach, there would have been concern at Anfield over the potential damage an Arsenal midfield of Declan Rice, Bruno Guimarães and Martin Ødegaard could inflict on Sunday. They still might, with Iraola saying his team need to improve “almost everywhere”. But talk of the midfield being frequently overrun has fallen silent during a winning run underpinned by aggression, resilience and intensity. Mac Allister has embodied it all. His negotiating position is strong once again.

articles.title: 10 spine-chilling places to visit in Britain for Halloween
articles.summary: Ghostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sites A derelict, 24-metre tall redbrick and flint folly outside Chichester, Racton Monument (known locally as Racton Ruin) is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex and has been the site of many paranormal investigations. George Montagu Dunk, the second Earl of Halifax, commissioned the folly, but there is no conclusive account as to why he had it built. Some say it was as a summerhouse, others a viewing point to watch ships come in from the Solent. A ghostly woman walking in the grounds and eerie sounds such as sudden manic laughter are among reported spooky happenings. Now completely gutted and roofless, it’s on private land and unsafe to enter, but still easily seen from nearby footpaths . Continue reading...
articles.content:
Ghostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sites

A derelict, 24-metre tall redbrick and flint folly outside Chichester, Racton Monument (known locally as Racton Ruin) is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex and has been the site of many paranormal investigations. George Montagu Dunk, the second Earl of Halifax, commissioned the folly, but there is no conclusive account as to why he had it built. Some say it was as a summerhouse, others a viewing point to watch ships come in from the Solent. A ghostly woman walking in the grounds and eerie sounds such as sudden manic laughter are among reported spooky happenings. Now completely gutted and roofless, it’s on private land and unsafe to enter, but still easily seen from nearby footpaths .

Completed in 1927, the Pontsticill reservoir in the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) national park supplies water for much of south Wales, holding up to 15.5 billion litres (3,400 million gallons). Like other reservoirs of its time, such as Ladybower in Derbyshire, Pontsticill was built with a bell-mouth spillway, which looks like an eerie giant plughole – or the event horizon of a black hole. Created by flooding a valley, ghostly remains of the submerged village, including a 15th-century church, can resurface during droughts when water levels drop. Richard Ayoade used its terrifying presence with great effect in his 2010 film, Submarine.

With place names such as Deadman’s Island, Slaughterhouse Point and Bedlam’s Bottom, Chetney Marshes needs no introduction. This forgotten, marshy outpost on the fringes of north Kent, with a limited palette of greens and greys, is home to a collection of slowly decaying, old barges and boats. Such is their level of deterioration, it can be hard to distinguish between the rotten hulks and the marsh itself. Information on the wrecked vessels is hard to come by and contradictory, with Historic England claiming they are former Thames barges. Yet on older maps, they are marked as the more tantalising Victorian prisoner transport ships. An atmospheric place for an otherworldly wander.

Growing up on terrifying visions of nuclear war, such as 1980s films Threads and Where the Wind Blows, bunkers have always held a certain macabre mystique. Kelvedon Hatch was one such bunker, built in the early 1950s to house up to 600 military personnel and civilians, as well as the prime minister. In this worst-case scenario, it would have become the seat of power in a post-apocalyptic Britain. Above the surface, it looks like an unremarkable bungalow, but, like a Bond villain’s lair, this leads to a three-storey underground shelter equivalent in size to 25 average British homes. Today, the bunker is home to one of the world’s largest cold war museums.

On a Pennine hill overlooking Burnley, the Singing Ringing Tree is an eerie sound sculpture created by architects Mike Tonkin and Anna Liu. It is three metres tall and designed to look like a brutalist windswept tree. The sculpture comprises a series of galvanised steel pipes tuned to various pitches over a range of different octaves. On a gusty day, as the wind blows through the pipes, it creates a weird, somewhat discordant harmonic. The artwork is one of four Panopticons , but rather than embodying the original concept – a circular prison with a single guard at its centre – they are far more benign, designed to be seen by many rather than as a symbol of oppressive surveillance.

Tucked away in the Tilberthwaite valley, between Coniston and Langdale, Ho dge Close is an abandoned slate quarry on National Trust land. In the right conditions, its cave tunnel openings and dark pool resemble a skull, which fans of the hit Netflix series The Witcher will recognise – though it’s much harder to see in real life than in the scenes starring Henry Cavill (Geralt of Rivia) and Kim Bodnia (Vesemir). Abandoned in the 1960s, industrial remains litter the site, giving it an edgy, post-civilisation feel.

Crossbones graveyard , just south of the River Thames near Shakespeare’s Globe theatre and the Shard, was once outside the city’s boundaries (and laws) in an area known as “The Liberty of the Clink”. A pauper’s graveyard, it was the final resting place of medieval sex workers and souls not deemed suitable for Christian burial. More than 15,000 people are estimated to have been unceremoniously buried here. Today, it’s been reclaimed as a garden of remembrance, both mystical and macabre with its own special beauty, and is open to the public at certain times for guided walks and talks.

Hundreds of years ago, Cateran Hole was used by bandits to hide smuggled contraband. Found in the middle of Bewick Moor, about four miles north of Eglingham, it feels as far away from civilisation as you can get, and the steps leading down to its 35 metre-long, dark underground chamber are notoriously difficult to find – making it all the more thrilling when you finally do. You can walk into increasing darkness if you’re brave enough, before the tunnel tapers to a narrow point, but be cautious: there are no safety barriers, lighting or warning signs.

We all know that strange feeling of being watched – then turning round to find nobody there. If you wander just off the Old Edinburgh Road in a beautiful, isolated corner of the Galloway Hills, not far from Newton Stewart, you’ll find a whole bunch of faces staring out at you from the confines of a drystone wall. Artist Matt Baker carved Quorum – the Stone Faces in 1997 as part of a residency in the Galloway Forest. The heads have since become part of the landscape and have even formed new eyebrows out of lichen. The artwork is a stone’s throw away from another impressive piece called The Eye , a 10-metre tall cone sculpture on the banks of Black Loch.

Arrive on a cold morning as the mist shrouds St Matthew’s church in Normanton , and it appears as if it is rising up from the depths of a lake. Normanton Church, as it is also known, stands on a small, boulder-strewn promontory on the vast expanse of Rutland Water. Built in the 1820s on the site of a medieval chapel, the church was scheduled for demolition when the man-made lake/reservoir was built in the 1970s. Thankfully, a last-minute public campaign saved it from this watery fate. Easy to view from the shoreline, it is open on scheduled days and for private events.

paragraphs: Ghostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sites

A derelict, 24-metre tall redbrick and flint folly outside Chichester, Racton Monument (known locally as Racton Ruin) is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex and has been the site of many paranormal investigations. George Montagu Dunk, the second Earl of Halifax, commissioned the folly, but there is no conclusive account as to why he had it built. Some say it was as a summerhouse, others a viewing point to watch ships come in from the Solent. A ghostly woman walking in the grounds and eerie sounds such as sudden manic laughter are among reported spooky happenings. Now completely gutted and roofless, it’s on private land and unsafe to enter, but still easily seen from nearby footpaths .

Completed in 1927, the Pontsticill reservoir in the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) national park supplies water for much of south Wales, holding up to 15.5 billion litres (3,400 million gallons). Like other reservoirs of its time, such as Ladybower in Derbyshire, Pontsticill was built with a bell-mouth spillway, which looks like an eerie giant plughole – or the event horizon of a black hole. Created by flooding a valley, ghostly remains of the submerged village, including a 15th-century church, can resurface during droughts when water levels drop. Richard Ayoade used its terrifying presence with great effect in his 2010 film, Submarine.

With place names such as Deadman’s Island, Slaughterhouse Point and Bedlam’s Bottom, Chetney Marshes needs no introduction. This forgotten, marshy outpost on the fringes of north Kent, with a limited palette of greens and greys, is home to a collection of slowly decaying, old barges and boats. Such is their level of deterioration, it can be hard to distinguish between the rotten hulks and the marsh itself. Information on the wrecked vessels is hard to come by and contradictory, with Historic England claiming they are former Thames barges. Yet on older maps, they are marked as the more tantalising Victorian prisoner transport ships. An atmospheric place for an otherworldly wander.

Growing up on terrifying visions of nuclear war, such as 1980s films Threads and Where the Wind Blows, bunkers have always held a certain macabre mystique. Kelvedon Hatch was one such bunker, built in the early 1950s to house up to 600 military personnel and civilians, as well as the prime minister. In this worst-case scenario, it would have become the seat of power in a post-apocalyptic Britain. Above the surface, it looks like an unremarkable bungalow, but, like a Bond villain’s lair, this leads to a three-storey underground shelter equivalent in size to 25 average British homes. Today, the bunker is home to one of the world’s largest cold war museums.

On a Pennine hill overlooking Burnley, the Singing Ringing Tree is an eerie sound sculpture created by architects Mike Tonkin and Anna Liu. It is three metres tall and designed to look like a brutalist windswept tree. The sculpture comprises a series of galvanised steel pipes tuned to various pitches over a range of different octaves. On a gusty day, as the wind blows through the pipes, it creates a weird, somewhat discordant harmonic. The artwork is one of four Panopticons , but rather than embodying the original concept – a circular prison with a single guard at its centre – they are far more benign, designed to be seen by many rather than as a symbol of oppressive surveillance.

Tucked away in the Tilberthwaite valley, between Coniston and Langdale, Ho dge Close is an abandoned slate quarry on National Trust land. In the right conditions, its cave tunnel openings and dark pool resemble a skull, which fans of the hit Netflix series The Witcher will recognise – though it’s much harder to see in real life than in the scenes starring Henry Cavill (Geralt of Rivia) and Kim Bodnia (Vesemir). Abandoned in the 1960s, industrial remains litter the site, giving it an edgy, post-civilisation feel.

Crossbones graveyard , just south of the River Thames near Shakespeare’s Globe theatre and the Shard, was once outside the city’s boundaries (and laws) in an area known as “The Liberty of the Clink”. A pauper’s graveyard, it was the final resting place of medieval sex workers and souls not deemed suitable for Christian burial. More than 15,000 people are estimated to have been unceremoniously buried here. Today, it’s been reclaimed as a garden of remembrance, both mystical and macabre with its own special beauty, and is open to the public at certain times for guided walks and talks.

articles.title: Rewilding project aims to restore peatland
articles.summary: Cumbria Wildlife Trust starts work repairing damage to Skiddaw Forest's peatland.
articles.content:
Work has started on a project to restore 435 hectares (1,077 acres) of damaged peatland.

Cumbria Wildlife Trust will carry out the work in Skiddaw Forest where it will also repair a 6km (3.7-mile) boundary fence.

The forest is home to one of the largest continuous areas of blanket bog in the Lake District and acts as a huge carbon store.

Peatland team manager for the trust Susie Webb said: "Once improved, the peatlands will also slow the flow of water off the fells, which will help protect local communities downstream from flooding and will benefit a huge variety of wildlife."

The project is expected to take between three and four months but public access to Skiddaw Forest won't be affected.

Webb said: "We expect to see an increase in specialist plants such as sundews and sphagnum mosses and greater numbers of dragonflies.

"Birds such as snipe, which live on wet grassland, marshes and moorlands, will benefit from the rewetted ground."

articles.title: Jackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured cream
articles.summary: Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat I love a tarte tatin: it’s one of those perfect recipes that contains only a few key ingredients at its core – in this case, butter, sugar, apples and pastry – yet it brings out the absolute best qualities from each: the sugar dark, bittersweet, caramelised, and tempered by the acidity of the apples, the texture softened but held by the combination of butter and fruit pectin. The only problem is that the whole thing happens behind a screen of puff pastry, meaning that tarte tatin takes a great deal of practice and repetition to reach the right level of caramelisation blind. So, here, I’ve dispensed with the pastry altogether, making it a much easier preparation. For the intrepid, this is delicious cooked over a bonfire, where the smoke adds an incredible extra dimension; it also functions as a warming treat after a chilly evening out watching the fireworks. Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London Continue reading...
articles.content:
Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat

I love a tarte tatin: it’s one of those perfect recipes that contains only a few key ingredients at its core – in this case, butter, sugar, apples and pastry – yet it brings out the absolute best qualities from each: the sugar dark, bittersweet, caramelised, and tempered by the acidity of the apples, the texture softened but held by the combination of butter and fruit pectin. The only problem is that the whole thing happens behind a screen of puff pastry, meaning that tarte tatin takes a great deal of practice and repetition to reach the right level of caramelisation blind. So, here, I’ve dispensed with the pastry altogether, making it a much easier preparation. For the intrepid, this is delicious cooked over a bonfire, where the smoke adds an incredible extra dimension; it also functions as a warming treat after a chilly evening out watching the fireworks.

This basically follows my method for making tarte tatin, but without the need for pastry – nor to turn out a pan of seething caramel at significant danger to the skin on your wrists. The butter and sugar in the presence of the apples produce a beautiful and slightly acidic toffee sauce, while the fruit retains enough bite to stand up for itself and avoid disintegrating into mush. By drying out the quartered fruit in the fridge first, you ensure a nice, even caramelisation of the sugar and helps the apples maintain their shape and integrity. That said, you can also dry them in an oven set to 80C (60C fan)/gas very low for 30 minutes.

6 apples – braeburn or discovery, for preference 100g unsalted butter , softened 100g caster sugar 500g soured cream , to serve A few pinches ground cinnamon , to serve 100g toasted walnuts , to serve

Peel the apples, cut them in half and then into quarters, then cut out and discard the cores. Put the apple pieces on a tray and leave uncovered in the fridge for two hours to dry out.

Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Press the butter all over the base of an ovenproof nonstick pan, so it covers the entire flat surface, then scatter the sugar evenly over the top. Arrange the apples cut-side up on top (I like to shape them into a fan), then put the pan on a medium heat to melt the butter and caramelise the sugar for five to 10 minutes, gently shaking the pan every few minutes, until the sugar has melted to a dark caramel. Transfer to the oven and bake for 30 minutes, until everything is deliciously brown and bubbling.

Remove, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then divide between warmed bowls and serve with a generous spoon of soured cream, a dusting of cinnamon and some toasted walnuts.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London
