articles.title: Blind date: ‘He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me’
articles.summary: Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketing What were you hoping for? Great company and wonderful conversation. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketing

First impressions? Louise is such a sweet, sincere person. With very interesting hobbies!

What did you talk about? All sorts of funny things, from feeding monkeys to the worst theatre shows and wooden toys.

Most awkward moment? When we met, I wanted to greet her with a friendly hug but she was seated and had to get up.

Good table manners? Impeccable, and she had amazing taco-eating skills.

Best thing about Louise? She will laugh and think I’m taking the mick but I’m not: her dedication to the things she loves. So admirable! Passion and commitment. It’s infectious.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian.com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here . What questions will I be asked? We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with? No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph? No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

How should I answer? Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers? No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Can I do it in my home town? Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

Describe Louise in three words Energetic, passionate, excellent conversationalist (four I know!).

What do you think Louise made of you? An oddball with similar interests?

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I wouldn’t change a thing! It was a very pleasant date overall.

What were you hoping for? Fun conversation with an interesting person and to discover a new restaurant.

First impressions? A gentleman, very polite, laughs very loudly (in a good way).

What did you talk about? London zoo volunteering – a typical day. Nelson growing up in Singapore. Covid – how I was in Singapore and Bali just as it started kicking off. Theatre shows we’ve been to – how perfect Oliver! is (this was mainly me). How we both go and see all the Oscar-nominated films every awards season. Nelson’s new startup.

Most awkward moment? The waitress thought a photographer would be joining us and we needed a table for three.

Good table manners? I was more conscious of my own, as I ate the tacos with my hands while he used cutlery.

Best thing about Nelson? He’s a very interesting and interested person – so many hobbies and passions. I liked that he shared my enthusiasm for all things cultural.

Would you introduce Nelson to your friends? Can’t think why not, he’s very interesting and sweet!

What do you think Nelson made of you? He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might just be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me. He also laughed very heartily all the way through so hopefully he thought I was funny.

Did you go on somewhere? No, but we were the last to leave on a Tuesday night, so pretty good going.

If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be? The pineapple/lime/cinnamon ice-cream was incredible, we should’ve got one each.

Would you meet again? I think as friends – maybe at the cinema as Oscar season is approaching!

Nelson and Louise ate at Mirtala , London W4. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

articles.title: Arteta can take inspiration from George Graham to expunge painful Anfield memories
articles.summary: Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nights Mikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011: bajar . “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.” Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood – could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenal in September 2012 , after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”. Continue reading...

Arsenal have not won at Liverpool for 13 league games but Gunners’ win in 1989 remains one of club’s greatest nights

M ikel Arteta used a Spanish word to describe what it felt like to be helpless at Anfield while playing for Everton in 2011: bajar . “It’s when a cyclist is going up and looks amazing, then in one kilometre he goes ‘boom’ and he’s struggling again,” he said in Amazon’s All or Nothing documentary. “The game was going well and then suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around. The game is passing all over me and I cannot react. I only had that feeling in my career once, and it was at Anfield.”

Given Arteta’s record at Liverpool, Sunday’s showdown with his childhood friend Andoni Iraola – five days after Arsenal were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Fleetwood – could be expected to fill him with dread. Arteta finally tasted victory there as a player with Arsenal in September 2012 , after five failed attempts in the Merseyside derby, but ended up spending the night in hospital with concussion after colliding with Jordan Henderson in an incident he has described as “the biggest fear of my life”.

Arteta was part of the Arsenal side that won at Anfield again six months later thanks to goals from the new signings Lukas Podolski and Santi Cazorla. That was the last time the club triumphed there in the Premier League. They have not won at Anfield for 13 league matches, equalling the club’s worst run at Liverpool. Arsenal’s one victory at Liverpool in the interim came in the League Cup on penalties in 2020 on Arteta’s second visit as a manager.

The Spaniard tried to prepare his players for a trip to Anfield in November 2021 by playing You’ll Never Walk Alone over the training ground speakers but that ended in a 4-0 defeat . He was criticised after last season’s loss in late August, when Dominik Szoboszlai’s late free-kick ended a sequence of three Arsenal draws at Liverpool, for a perceived failure to take off the handbrake, having started Mikel Merino as his No 10. Gary Neville went as far as to say Arsenal lacked “the mentality to go and win big matches at big away grounds”, an assertion that will have hurt Arteta but does have credence: they have not beaten Manchester City in the Premier League at the Etihad since 2015 under Arsène Wenger.

Arteta will be keen to disprove such perceptions, especially after Arsenal struggled so badly against a team 84 places below them in the pyramid in a stadium that holds fewer than 6,000 people. The strikers Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyökeres surprisingly started in tandem at Fleetwood, presumably in an attempt to lighten the load on Martin Ødegaard, although both look badly out of form. Bukayo Saka is out with a thigh injury , there are concerns over Noni Madueke’s ankle and Arsenal’s failed appeal over Max Dowman’s red card rules out the teenager for three matches.

With that in mind, Arteta’s best chance of beating Liverpool is probably by taking the cautious approach that has served him so well and was the cornerstone of last season’s Premier League title triumph. He can take inspiration from one of the most famous nights in Arsenal’s history 37 years ago when George Graham’s side arrived at Anfield needing a 2-0 victory to be champions.

“I told my players to keep things tight in the first half – it was imperative we did not concede,” said Graham in an interview to mark the 20th anniversary of that dramatic finale to the 1988-89 season, when Michael Thomas scored in stoppage time to end Arsenal’s 18-year wait for the title. “The papers were saying we’d have to attack from the off, but I was adamant that was wrong. If Liverpool had scored an early goal it would have been over. But they did very little attacking and played into our hands.”

Before the 1989 game, Arsenal’s players ran to all four corners of the ground to hand flowers to Liverpool fans as a show of sympathy after the Hillsborough disaster the previous month – an idea proposed by their longstanding director Ken Friar, who died this month.

Graham and Arteta were 44 when they won their first league titles and the similarities do not end there. The former Scotland midfielder, who scored almost 80 goals for Arsenal and helped them win the Double in 1971, was known for his emphasis on defending as a manager and “1-0 to the Arsenal” became synonymous with Graham, especially towards the end of his reign. Arteta has revived that tradition since he took over in December 2019, recording 1-0 victories 32 times in the Premier League , more than any club apart from Everton.

Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal of the season in a routine 2-0 win at home to Everton last Saturday and targeting Liverpool’s weakness from set plays while keeping things tight at the other end could be the most effective tactic against a team who have been finding their feet under Iraola in recent weeks.

“Collectively, we acknowledge the importance of defending,” said Arteta last year when asked about comparisons between his team and Graham’s. “We know that if we excel in that part of the game, the chances and the probabilities to win more matches is going to be very, very high.”

Arsenal flew back to London after losing to Fleetwood on penalties in a shootout that will have revived bad memories of May’s Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain .

The Carabao Cup has stretched Arteta’s squad in the past two seasons, when they reached first the semi-finals then the final, so that is one potential positive from their elimination – not that the ultra-competitive Spaniard would agree. For him, the only way to respond to the most embarrassing night of his managerial career will be to follow in Graham’s footsteps on Sunday.

articles.content:
It influenced The Simpsons and sparked the careers of Eugene Levy, Catherine O’Hara, John Candy and many others. Now this extraordinary Canadian series is finally getting its due

S CTV – short for Second City Television – is one of most influential comedy shows ever created. In the 1970s and 80s, while North American comedy fans worshipped at the altar of Saturday Night Live, the comedy nerds loved SCTV. The Canadian sketch show was weird. It was dark. It was multilayered and years ahead of its time.

Dave Thomas, head writer and an original cast member, was there from the start. “Conan O’Brien said that he used to watch and he thought, ‘This show is being written specifically for me,’” Thomas tells me. “There were references in it that he was absolutely sure only he got. We wrote at the top of our reference level. And the idea was to see if the audience would meet us there.”

Thomas was part of an astonishingly talented cast that included John Candy, Eugene Levy , Catherine O’Hara , Rick Moranis, Joe Flaherty, Martin Short, Harold Ramis and Andrea Martin. They wrote and starred in the series, which ran intermittently in Canada from 1976 to 1984. At a time when American shows dominated the airwaves, and homegrown content tended to be earnest factual programmes along the lines of Hinterland Who’s Who , Canadian audiences were delighted to see a show that reflected their culture while being – to everyone’s surprise – actually funny. It even went on to find a late-night audience in the US.

To celebrate its legacy, Netflix has just added 134 episodes of SCTV to coincide with its release of a new documentary – SCTV: The Greatest Show You’ve Never Heard Of. Like many of the show’s fans, Thomas isn’t exactly enamoured with the title.

That’s not the only problem. While it’s a decent primer for revisiting the show, featuring new interviews with the surviving cast members, including Thomas, the documentary could have been so much more. Many things are skipped over, such as the musical acts, including bands like the Boomtown Rats and the Plasmatics, who didn’t just perform but also appeared in sketches. And while the cast took care of the writing in the show’s early days, they were later joined by talented staff. These omissions rankle with Thomas.

“Tom Hanks and Bob Odenkirk doing the narrative on how it was written? I thought, what the fuck? Why don’t you ask some of the people who wrote it? We had some really good writers on that show.”

There is a cracking story to be told. For the uninitiated: the cast of Chicago’s legendary Second City improv theatre had already been plundered by producer Lorne Michaels to create Saturday Night Live in 1975. It seemed to make perfect sense to use Second City’s Toronto outpost to create a Canadian version of SNL. Gilda Radner and Dan Aykroyd had already been poached by Michaels, so the remaining cast members were asked to make a television sketch show without knowing the first thing about it.

“For the first two seasons, SCTV was a failure,” Thomas remembers. “It was the poor brother of SNL. Our greatest weakness was that our show looked cheap as shit. So we made it about a small television station, and that’s why it looks so cheap.”

Each episode of SCTV covered one broadcast day for a run-down TV station in the fictional rural Canadian town of Melonville. As well as parodying the film and TV of the time, the backstage dramas of the station also played a part.

“We were learning,” Thomas tells me. “We were being paid to learn how to produce television while doing it. It really was the idiots running the asylum for the first two years. There are a lot of things we got credit for that were just horrible mistakes.”

The naivety of the cast and the low budget, paradoxically, freed up the sketch-writers: without shiny sets and special effects, they focused on characters. There was the overbearing station manager Guy Caballero , the cheapskate’s cheapskate; the garrulous variety star Johnny LaRue , who was an extension of John Candy’s party-loving nature; Catherine O’Hara’s showgirl Lola Heatherton ; Eugene Levy’s appalling standup, Bobby Bittman ; and Harry, the Guy With a Snake on his Face. Sketches were smart, sharp and featured startlingly accurate impressions ( Thomas’s Bob Hope was a standout).

As time went on, the show found its feet, started gaining an audience, increased its budget and grew more sophisticated.

“I was particularly proud of the evolution of the comedy,” Thomas remembers. “Like the parody of the television show Fantasy Island, which was also a parody of Casablanca, and also a parody of Road to Morocco, and also a parody of The Wizard of Oz, all weaved in and out. A lot of the Simpsons writers said that’s what they loved about SCTV, that it brought in a kind of a multilayered writing. And they said: that’s the way we write The Simpsons.”

But as the money came in, the creators’ freedom dwindled. Used to having everything their own way, the cast and writers baulked when threatened with any outside interference.

“I remember one of the producers that NBC had sent up was in the cafeteria one morning, crying,” recalls Thomas. “I said, ‘What’s the matter?’ He goes, ‘The goddamn cast, they shut me out. They stonewall me. I’ve got a good mind to quit.’ And I said, ‘Well, you probably should quit because you’re here in the cafeteria, crying. Is that what you had in mind when you got into showbiz?’”

Being produced in isolation gave SCTV a distinct personality and a legion of devoted fans. But the team were still very much on the outside.

“We went to New York for a press conference,” Thomas says. “There were only three people there and two of them were student journalists. But we thought, well, screw this press conference, let’s go to Studio 54. We’re on television. We should be able to get in. They wouldn’t let us in.”

Thomas and Rick Moranis (later to star in Ghostbusters, with Harold Ramis, and Honey, I Shrunk the Kids) were part of SCTV’s most surprising breakout success. Asked to include more specifically Canadian content in the series, they improvised two-minute pieces to camera featuring two dim-witted, beer-swilling, hockey-watching Canucks, Bob and Doug McKenzie. The characters caught on: Canadians, so used to watching American stereotypes played for laughs on TV, loved seeing two of their own get the same treatment. The documentary shows Beatles-like levels of hysteria at McKenzie brother appearances. They went on to record albums and make a film.

Not everyone in the cast was delighted by all this, as Thomas admits. “There’s no question that the success of the McKenzie brothers was a divisive factor and played a role in Rick and I leaving. There were little things like that which definitely sowed some seeds of division, but we were still family.”

The show shifted networks, time slots and cast members until it eventually fizzled out in 1984. But the SCTV family went on to greater heights. John Candy became a Hollywood star. Eugene Levy and Catherine O’Hara featured in many of Christopher Guest’s comedies (including Best in Show and A Mighty Wind), as well as starring in Schitt’s Creek together. Martin Short is, well, Martin Short.

And Thomas has a wildly varied career: he starred in the sitcom Grace Under Fire, wrote Spies Like Us with Dan Aykroyd, started an animation company and is now developing an Amazon show with his son. But Thomas will always be fiercely proud of his SCTV achievements.

“I loved that show because, I thought, nobody’s doing this. Nobody is doing a show like this. There was a network tendency to dumb everything down to the stupidest person in the room. And we didn’t do that.”

articles.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
articles.summary: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer , as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing . But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material. articles.content:
Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned

But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

Waine and Cutting claim their app can generate images depicting the supernatural, using signals from a phone’s built-in magnetometer, identifying words and phrases in those signals, and then running them through an image generator.

Fellow paranormal enthusiasts can post the images they generate to a feed and comment on other users’ pictures. Since its release in 2023, Seer has become a regular part of their onscreen work. In a recent video on their Amy’s Crypt YouTube channel, the pair sat in a carefully selected location in the Winchester Mystery House while running GhostTube Seer.

“Can you show us what used to go on in this room?” Cutting asked. The app generated an abstract compilation of wooden walls and golden curtains that the pair suggested could be one of the home’s bedrooms. Seer also generated images of humans and animals while running: a woman reading, another woman with a black shawl, and a flock of white birds flying. Each was interpreted by the pair to have some relevance to the history of the home. The pursuit of ghosts has historically been relatively niche and personal, even after early 2000s TV shows like Ghost Hunters prompted a surge of interest in the hobby. That’s changed in recent years. Ghost stories and sightings, once they find their way online, can become training material for large language models like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, just like any other content.

New technologies have always been a part of paranormal history, says Alex Matsuo, a paranormal researcher and author whose day job is in the technology industry. Thomas Edison’s attempt at a “spirit phone” to contact the dead is an early example, one with an ambition not dissimilar to today’s AI-powered “ deathbots ”. The history of spirit photographs, a hotly debated phenomenon of the 19th and early 20th century, parallels advances in new photography techniques.

Some paranormal enthusiasts, though, are concerned that generative AI is more than just another new technology to play with and instead threatens the soul of what they do. “I’m not surprised that AI has been embraced by a lot of people in the ghost hunting community,” said Matsuo.

When GhostTube Seer was first released, she tried it out. She is skeptical of what she’s seen so far.

“Any time someone’s coming out with a ghost hunting tool using AI, my big question has always been: ‘OK if you’re using AI, you’re using some sort of large language model, what data are you training it on to [determine] what’s a ghost?’” Matsuo said. She also noted that there are ethical concerns: is a generative image tool using copyrighted art to create its own spectres? Are ghost hunting chatbots sending users into their own “paranormal echo chambers”?

Other paranormal enthusiasts are embracing the proverbial ghost in the machine. Seer isn’t the only generative AI app designed for ghost hunters. Sean Austin, a paranormal investigator who was featured on a Travel Channel series about ghost hunting, launched an app called Spirit Phone Innovations that uses “advanced AI” to analyze audio signals to detect EVP – electronic voice phenomena – a mainstay of ghost hunting.

Matsuo believes the heart of looking for ghosts should remain deeply human.

“A lot of us come into the ghost hunting world because we’ve gone through some trauma or grief,” she said. Ghost hunting is, for many, a form of processing loss, she said. “Everyone’s trying to find the next big thing that could give us an answer into the unknown or validating the existence of ghosts.”

As AI’s physical footprint expands with the rapid construction of datacenters across the US, ghostly locations are likewise facing the threat of change. A former asylum in Pennsylvania that became a beloved haunted house was sold to a datacenter developer in late 2025 to be torn down. However, local residents banded together and successfully blocked it in May.

articles.title: Seth Meyers on Trump and Vance’s tactics: ‘No one’s buying your fake folksy bullshit’
articles.summary: Late-night hosts criticised ‘cosplaying as everyday folks’ and mocked the president’s latest attack on a reporter Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump and JD Vance for their hollow attempts to appeal to working-class voters while also detailing the president’s latest unhinged attack on a reporter. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Late-night hosts criticised ‘cosplaying as everyday folks’ and mocked the president’s latest attack on a reporter

Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump and JD Vance for their hollow attempts to appeal to working-class voters while also detailing the president’s latest unhinged attack on a reporter.

On Late Night, Seth Meyers said that Republicans had been “cosplaying as regular, everyday folks” for a while, showing clips of Donald Trump working at McDonald’s and the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, claiming to be a soybean farmer.

This week the right continued to lose their minds over a joke made by Barack Obama, comparing Trump’s White House to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.

They were less bothered about the comparison to a “violent oppressive dictator” and more about a perceived slight towards a popular restaurant chain, organising an unsuccessful press opportunity outside one that Bessent was visiting.

Obama responded with more jabs, leading Meyers to say that “standup comedy Obama is back” and joked that his next special will be called Hussein in the Membrane.

Meyers also quipped that Rudy Guiliani “missed it because he showed up at the Cheesecake Factory Total Landscaping”.

Meyers called it “rightwing fan fiction” that Trump was a “true man of the people”, a claim that was “such obvious bullshit”.

This week also saw JD Vance claim that he can’t pronounce the names of countries in the Middle East when talking to audience members at a rally.

“No one’s buying your fake folksy bullshit,” Meyers said, reminding his viewers how rich and entitled Vance is.

He did joke that “if Trump said he couldn’t pronounce the names then I would believe that” then playing a clip of him stumbling over countries.

The right has also been obsessing over James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in Texas who “isn’t a real American because he secretly doesn’t like meat” with Trump claiming he is a vegan yet mispronouncing the word.

“Trump’s just gone full goblin now,” he said after playing a strange clip of him talking about meat.

Yet it was “not the most bizarre insult” from the right, with Ted Cruz saying that if you picked 1,000 adjectives for Talarico, the list wouldn’t include the word masculine.

“Do you think you’re masculine just because you grew 65% of a beard?” he asked.

There have also been some “truly revolting attacks” on the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, with Republicans calling him many things including a jihadist.

“It’s disgusting how nakedly racist this is,” Meyers said before adding that it “seems like these tactics are backfiring” given poll numbers.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about Trump having a tantrum after a reporter asked him if he was feeling well given a last-minute change in his schedule.

“Natalie, baby’s cranky again, we need a diaper change on runway two,” he said before adding “imagine him calling someone else out of shape”.

Kimmel suggested someone taking “him out to that reflecting pool” so he can see himself, adding that it was the “pot calling the belly fat”.

His rallies “used to be Team Trump through and through” yet more and more interlopers have found their way in. This week saw an Ohio heckler shout that Trump went on “the Jeffrey Epstein plane” and his fans responded with boos.

Trump has continued to brag about passing his cognitive tests, something “they give old people to make sure they can wipe themselves”.

He also played clips of Obama responding to the outrage over the Cheesecake Factory joke saying that we “traded in a Ferrari for a folding chair”.

Kimmel joked that, for Trump, the Cheesecake Factory menu was the “closest he gets to reading a book”.

This week has also seen Trump’s infamously terrible ex-press secretary Katie Zacharia “trying to repair her image” with a string of interviews, including a disastrous one with Piers Morgan.

Kimmel played footage of her “glitching” when trying to avoid a question, saying that someone should “maybe unplug her and plug her back in”.

articles.title: Sampa the Great: Nu Zamrock review – a full-circle moment for a world-class act

articles.content:
Sampa Tembo’s genre-hopping third album meets the moment with charisma and cheek

I n 2019, as Sampa the Great, Sampa Tembo became the first woman to win an Australian Recording Industry Association award for hip-hop or rap; she’s also the first (and only) person to win the Australian music prize twice. But she’s said consistently over the past decade that, while her music career began in Australia – when she was based here between 2013 and 2019 – she is still Zambian-born, Botswana-raised.

Having returned to Africa to live and record, she told the Guardian in 2022 : “I was constantly being called Australian. I felt that I really had to defend Zambia and Zambian music and culture. The fact I was raised in Botswana and heard this music as I was being raised there fell to the wayside.”

Does Australia’s eagerness to claim her as Our Sampa come in the same earnestly admiring spirit as we claim other imports whose careers took off from an Australian launchpad, like, say, Crowded House or Rebecca Gibney? Or is there an ugly, acquisitive streak in the disproportionately white Australian music industry that rushes to congratulate itself for “producing” “diaspora artists” like Tembo, who make our national creative output feel less stale and pale?

With the sounds of amapiano and Afrobeats entering the global pop charts via artists like Tyla and Burna Boy, mainstream western audiences are beginning to have a better grasp of the unique qualities and context of African pop and rock fusion genres, not to mention a better understanding that music was not invented in Liverpool in 1960.

In Nu Zamrock, Tembo also seems to call out peers who only start repping the culture when the mainstream catches on: “You’ll find me in Africa winding my waist / You ever been global? You just in the States,” she sneers on Location, nodding to her own explorations of the world: “Switching the game like a young relocation / Find me in Ghana and not on vacation.”

Her move back to Zambia , and her discovery of her family connection to Zamrock codifiers WITCH, also heavily informed and framed her 2022 album, As Above, So Below, and at first it’s a little hard to discern what is supposed to be “Nu” about her approach. But the full-circle feeling of her blend of blends – the tidal wave of psych-rock influence that has travelled the globe from the UK and the US in the 60s, to 70s Zambia, to Australia, through modern jazz and soul, all the way back to southern Africa – settles in beautifully on repeat listens, tumbling even more of those distinctive polyrhythms, kalindula and raw, high-gain guitar fuzz in alongside the self-possessed snap of her lyrical style. Collapsing genre further, she stacks repeated references to being an African and Zambian “rock star”. It’s as though she has relaxed a little as both a performer and producer – the way you can when surrounded by people for whom you don’t have to perform an identity – without sacrificing any discipline.

Through her sonic evolution she remains thematically consistent: Nu Zamrock is at least the third of her records to contain lyrical nods to the concept of “a seat at the table”, and she gives us an update on the “demons” she described at her heels on Shadows, the opening track to As Above, in the stomping Simon Says: “I say all my demons is dead.”

The early single Can’t Hold Us is a sync-ready anthem about resilience featuring her sister Mwanje; the unflinching Canary hits like a truck; while the lush Catch If You Can lets the listener catch a breath. A guest spot from Sia in Supernova fits surprisingly well – there is a rat-a-tat quality to their respective deliveries that works beautifully – but not even Sampa’s charisma is a match for the pop juggernaut’s steamrolling, blocky toplines. Tembo has never sought commercial approval but the softer tracks here remove any doubt that she could crush pop music if she wanted to.

Later, on Star, she croons affirmation to someone who might be wondering how to get from the crowd to the stage: “Did you know you could be just the way you are, love / To be someone like me?”

Nu Zamrock is the sound of Tembo telling the industry that how it chooses to perceive her is none of her business . Whereas back in 2018 she wondered “How you supposed to be Black down under?” on Simon Says she now shrugs cheekily: “Sampa the Great is the problem I’m waiting for them to solve.” For her, delivering a world-class view of a widescreen world is no problem at all.

articles.title: Mercury, lead and methanol found in counterfeit beauty products seized across UK
articles.summary: Copies of popular cosmetics and skincare products more likely to contain toxic substances, Trading Standards warns Mercury, lead and methanol have been found in counterfeit beauty products seized across the UK, Trading Standards has said. There is a rising problem with fake beauty products, with scammers selling copies of popular and expensive brands. Cosmetics, skincare and perfumes are now among the watchdog’s most commonly investigated fakes. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Copies of popular cosmetics and skincare products more likely to contain toxic substances, Trading Standards warns

Mercury, lead and methanol have been found in counterfeit beauty products seized across the UK, Trading Standards has said.

There is a rising problem with fake beauty products, with scammers selling copies of popular and expensive brands. Cosmetics, skincare and perfumes are now among the watchdog’s most commonly investigated fakes.

Tests found 13,200 parts per million of mercury in one skincare product, high levels of lead in lipstick, eyeshadow and contour products, nicotine in perfume and a counterfeit fragrance made up of about 80% methanol , a toxic alcohol that can cause serious poisoning.

About 20% of 18- to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly bought counterfeits, up from 6% in 2023, according to the latest Intellectual Property Office (IPO) counterfeit goods tracker.

Counterfeit products are more likely to contain harmful substances because they do not have to undergo health and safety tests or contain accurate ingredient lists. Surveys by Trading Standards found that nearly three in four people who bought counterfeit cosmetics and toiletries did so online.

The Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products including hair extensions, shampoo and conditioners in July. Another raid in Bolton by Trading Standards officers uncovered £2m worth of counterfeit goods, including perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes at a production facility in a commercial property.

Trading Standards tested a cross-section of 50 seized counterfeit cosmetic products and identified potentially harmful substances. Mercury is being increasingly found in skincare, and repeated exposure through the skin can damage the kidneys and nervous system.

Some counterfeit makeup including lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products were found to contain high levels of lead, which can damage the brain, nervous system and kidneys, with particular risks for children and during pregnancy.

Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: “Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally and those effects may not be immediately obvious.

“Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made or what risk it might pose. That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters.”

Helen Barnham, the head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: “These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. Products can look remarkably convincing but, behind the packaging, they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions.

“Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet.”

The IPO is launching a campaign called Face the Fakes, working with content creators and the beauty industry to highlight the harms of counterfeit products.

Millie Kendall, the chief executive of the British Beauty Council, said: “The UK beauty industry puts enormous care, creativity and expertise into creating products that people love and can use with confidence. Safety and trust run right through our industry, from the brands developing products to the retailers and professionals bringing them to consumers.

“Counterfeiters trade on the reputation and creativity that brilliant beauty businesses have worked hard to build, without putting in the same care or meeting the same standards. We are proud to support Face the Fakes and stand alongside businesses across our industry to help consumers buy beauty with confidence and keep fakes out of their beauty bags.”

Counterfeit products are more likely to contain harmful substances because they do not have to undergo health and safety tests or contain accurate ingredient lists. Surveys by Trading Standards found that nearly three in four people who bought counterfeit cosmetics and toiletries did so online.

The Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products including hair extensions, shampoo and conditioners in July. Another raid in Bolton by Trading Standards officers uncovered £2m worth of counterfeit goods, including perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes at a production facility in a commercial property.

Trading Standards tested a cross-section of 50 seized counterfeit cosmetic products and identified potentially harmful substances. Mercury is being increasingly found in skincare, and repeated exposure through the skin can damage the kidneys and nervous system.

Some counterfeit makeup including lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products were found to contain high levels of lead, which can damage the brain, nervous system and kidneys, with particular risks for children and during pregnancy.

Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: “Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally and those effects may not be immediately obvious.

“Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made or what risk it might pose. That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters.”

Helen Barnham, the head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: “These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. Products can look remarkably convincing but, behind the packaging, they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions.
“Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet.”
The IPO is launching a campaign called Face the Fakes, working with content creators and the beauty industry to highlight the harms of counterfeit products.

Millie Kendall, the chief executive of the British Beauty Council, said: “The UK beauty industry puts enormous care, creativity and expertise into creating products that people love and can use with confidence. Safety and trust run right through our industry, from the brands developing products to the retailers and professionals bringing them to consumers.

“Counterfeiters trade on the reputation and creativity that brilliant beauty businesses have worked hard to build, without putting in the same care or meeting the same standards. We are proud to support Face the Fakes and stand alongside businesses across our industry to help consumers buy beauty with confidence and keep fakes out of their beauty bags.”

articles.title: Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
articles.summary: Binance has been hit by what could be the biggest crypto hack ever - here's what we know so far
articles.content:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).

Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.

Binance says it is beginning to recover crypto funds after $6.3bn hack thought to be largest ever

Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.

The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.

Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.

From Bitcoin to blockchain: Key cryptocurrency terms and what they mean

The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com.

Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.

In an initial announcement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.

"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."

He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".

Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".

Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".

Teng has since said the hack was "not carried out by one person" and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".

"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.

Binance co-chief executive officer Richard Teng speaks at a conference

It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.

These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.

North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".

Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.

Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".

North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.

In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.

He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.

Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far.

Teng said concerned users can check funds on their Binance accounts. Experts suggest doing so through the official app and website, and to reach out to the company's customer service with any questions.

Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.

Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".

"Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said.

"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."

Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".

"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.

"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."

She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.

Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.

The Bank of England has warned , external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.

Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.

But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.

According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

articles.content:
Vivian Beaumont theater, New York City Unconvincing performances and an ill-fitting big stage make a retooled version of the classic courtroom drama feel like a missed opportunity

G iven the current state of the US military brass, it makes some sense that audiences would want to drift back to an older, nobler idea of the armed services, in which bad actors exist but are rooted out by the good guys in uniform. That perhaps explains the Broadway revival of A Few Good Men, Aaron Sorkin’s 1989 courtroom drama about a cocky military attorney defending two young marines who followed an illegal order with fatal results. The play is at once sharp and misty-eyed, critiquing a hallowed institution while reverently imbuing it with a certain dignity – in some ways, it does for the military what Sorkin’s The West Wing did for the Oval Office.

A Few Good Men was turned into a hit Oscar-nominated film in 1992, starring a then boyish Tom Cruise in the role of recalcitrant navy lawyer Daniel Kaffee and a frightening Jack Nicholson as Kaffee’s ultimate enemy, Colonel Jessep, the hardliner in command of the US military base at Guantánamo Bay, where a marine has died under troubling circumstances. Directed by Rob Reiner, the film is a clever, old-fashioned crowd pleaser, culminating in a classic trial scene punctuated by the line. “You can’t handle the truth!”, Jessep memorably bellows at Kaffee just before confessing to his misdeeds. Those in search of crackling drama and sentimentality about the military should just watch that film, rather than plunking down a considerable sum of money to see the play in its current form at Lincoln Center’s Vivian Beaumont theater.

The production is helmed by Michael Arden, an actor turned director who is no stranger to courtroom intrigue: he was behind the lovely 2023 revival of the musical Parade, about a wrongly accused man standing trial for murder. But that show had songs to rely on, whereas A Few Good Men has only its complicated Sorkin dialogue to propel it along. Arden proves less adept at turning that fast talk into music; in his hands, the play is lurching and awkward, rarely finding the rhythm necessary to keep Sorkin’s verbosity afloat.

It doesn’t help that the Beaumont is an enormous space, and Arden and scenic designer Dane Laffrey do nothing to make it more intimate. They use nearly the whole depth of the stage, and highlight the proscenium’s height with looming beams and a guard tower meant to evoke Jessep’s outpost in Cuba. That volume effectively swallows up the rapid, close chatter of the play, rendering it all quiet and tinny. We feel little of the propulsive charge of the story, as Kaffee navigates setbacks and, in the process, finds the principled conviction his career had previously lacked. There is a curious diffuseness to this A Few Good Men, the sense that we are watching the dim memory of something that was once exciting, rather than the thing itself.

Perhaps an actor of sturdier stock than Tom Blyth could have made things more resonant. As Kaffee, Blyth – a 31-year-old Briton most famous for a 2023 Hunger Games prequel film – has the arrogant, golden-boy strut down pretty well. But he struggles to convincingly convey Kaffee’s legal acumen, his cunning in getting the desired result from a cornered witness. As dogged internal affairs attorney Joanne Galloway (played by Demi Moore in the film), musical theater mainstay Krysta Rodriguez has similar problems of gravitas – she’s a bright presence, but one does begin to wonder what a plucky ingenue from a 1940s romp is doing at a court-martial.

The real sore spot in the ensemble, though, is a direly miscast Bradley Whitford as Jessep, a role that should radiate imperious menace, but in Whitford’s rendition comes across confused and unfocused. Whitford totters around the stage with his legs wide apart, as if he is doing a creaky John Wayne impression. He half mumbles and half growls his lines, a strained simulation of macho might. Whitford proved in two separate television series that he can more than handle Sorkin’s signature patter. (He’s also now doing great work on the Sorkin-esque series The Diplomat.) But Jessep is not one of Sorkin’s zippy smart guys. He’s a bull, a bear, something atavistic and scary. That’s not exactly in Whitford’s wheelhouse, it seems.

This clash of actor and part would be more tolerable if, in the performance I saw, Whitford seemed more confident with his lines. Blyth also struggled in that regard, particularly in the climactic scene in which Kaffee provokes Jessep into disclosing the real truth of the matter on the stand. While attempting to summit the peak of the play, both actors stumbled over their words and, on a few occasions, seemed to go blank for a moment. Which killed any momentum that Arden had managed to whip up; the scene came and went at a limping stagger and then the story huffed to a close. Hopefully Whitford and Blyth have fared better at other performances, but even then I doubt that this A Few Good Men generated much heat or electricity. It’s a starchy, listless production that never finds a proper sense of scale.

Not all is lost, though. There are some great turns from actors in smaller roles, including Nick Blaemire as a wise-cracking and morally concerned second-chair lawyer; Thom Sesma as a conflicted lieutenant colonel; and Michael Oberholtzer as the lead prosecutor on the case. They find the right cadence and timbre to make Sorkin’s ornate language sound casual and credible. If only they were in a smaller theater – where audiences could really feel the cramp of the courtroom, the pressure of a military base – and led by more suitable stars. As is, they are but a few good players in a production disappointingly derelict in its duty.

A Few Good Men is at Vivian Beaumont theater, New York City, until 10 January 2027

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe
articles.summary: A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in Senegal About 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. articles.content:
A historical adventure deep in the very heart of pasta country in southern Italy unexpectedly unearths a sauce with roots in Senegal

A bout 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano.

The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.

The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.

Often in strings hung over wooden frames, pasta was dried in the streets of Gragnano, then moved inside when necessary; the skill of the pasta makers and their ability to harness the weather every bit as important as the weather itself. And the industry grew. According to the city of Gragnano website, by 1859 there were 81 pasta factories, requiring ever increasing amounts of hard durum wheat for their pasta, while the mills produced soft wheat. The mills ceased operations in the 1950s, and were largely abandoned until renovation projects turned some of them into small museums.

What has continued to grow in Gragnano, though, is the tradition and art of pasta making; now with its own Indicazione Geografica Protetta, which protects its quality (provenance of wheat, how it is extruded, how long it is dried) and connection with the region. These days, 23 producers – from tiny to vast, 15 of which make up a consortium – make more than 100,000 tonnes of pasta annually in carefully controlled conditions – conditions very different from the open streets, but requiring just as much skill. I returned to Rome with bags of pasta from seven different makers – Di Martino, Faella, Garofalo, Liguori, Afeltra, Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Ducato d’Amalfi – all of which pleased me with their nutty scent, porous texture and resilience in the pan.

I also came back from Gragnano with a recipe devised for the town’s Mondopasta festival this year by chef Astou Ndiaye. Born in Dakar and now living with her family in Milan, Ndiaye’s cooking draws both on her heritage and her home. For her beautiful Senegalese ragu, the meat (I used lamb) is marinated in an aromatic blend of vegetables, coriander and cloves before being braised for a stew soft enough to be pasta sauce. I used candel e (hollow tubes) made by Garofalo, which I broke into short lengths. It’s a dish that sums up the spirit of pasta di Gragnano, I think; rooted in both Gragnano and Dakar, and at home anywhere.

1 stick celery, trimmed 1 small red pepper, trimmed, deseeded and cut into strips 1 shallot, peeled 1 small bunch coriander 2 garlic cloves, peeled 3 cloves Salt 600g boned lamb shoulder, cubed Olive oil 1 large onion, peeled and diced 1 tsp paprika 1 tsp garam masala 400-500g pasta (broken candele, maccheroni, mezze maniche)

Working in a food processor, pulse the celery, red pepper, shallot, coriander, garlic, cloves and a pinch of salt into a rough mixture. Put half the mixture into a bowl, add the meat, then toss so all the chunks are coated. Cover and leave to sit for two to 24 hours (if it’s three hours or more, put it in the fridge).

Working in a large, heavy-based pan, warm four teaspoons of olive oil. Working in batches, brown the marinated meat, then lift out on to a plate.

Add the diced onions to the empty pan, along with the remaining blended mixture and marinade, paprika and garam masala, and stir well, adding more water if it seems too dry. Add the meat, stir again, then add 300ml water. Bring to a simmer, then cover for two hours. By the end of cooking, the meat should be extremely tender and falling apart in just a little thick gravy.

In a separate pot, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions. Meanwhile, put half of the ragu into the bottom of a warm serving bowl. Lift the cooked, drained pasta on top, toss, adding more ragu as needed, then toss again.

This article was amended on 30 October 2026 to correct misspellings of pasta makers Garofalo and Ducato d’Amalfi.

articles.title: Is having urine the color of Mountain Dew normal?
articles.summary: A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say A doctor who advises several Trump cabinet members on their diets rhapsodized this summer about having urine the color of Mountain Dew, thanks to a diet consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. What you consume does determine what you see in the toilet. But should urine be neon yellow – or some other hue? Here’s what you need to know. Continue reading...
articles.content:
A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say

A doctor who advises several Trump cabinet members on their diets rhapsodized this summer about having urine the color of Mountain Dew, thanks to a diet consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods.

What you consume does determine what you see in the toilet. But should urine be neon yellow – or some other hue? Here’s what you need to know.

Urine is normally a shade of yellow owing to a pigment called urobilin, which your gut bacteria produce. The more diluted it is by extra fluid intake, the lighter its shade – so urine is typically darker in the morning or when you’re dehydrated.

You may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine “should” be, but “they are considered imprecise” and experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney disease, says Suzanne Watnick, a nephrologist at the University of Washington. Urine’s darkness or lightness loosely corresponds with hydration status, but for most people, it’s best to rely on your sense of thirst rather than what’s in the toilet to determine when to drink water.

That said, in people who need to stay highly hydrated, urine shade can be a helpful hydration indicator. For example, people prone to kidney stones should aim for very pale urine, Watnick says.

Your kidneys constantly filter blood to remove excess water and waste products , which trickle down to the bladder to get peed out as urine. These organs’ goal is to ensure your blood consistently has exactly the right balance of fluid, minerals, salts and acid.

“Your kidneys are really smart,” says Sharon Moe, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine. As long as they’re healthy, you can’t really override their settings. For instance, if you consume more water-soluble nutrients than you need, anything “extra” ends up in the toilet. This includes the byproducts your body makes when it breaks down food and medicines, as well as the majority of any vitamins and supplements you might be taking.

Some of these compounds won’t visibly change urine – for instance, digesting a lot of beef is likely to turn urine more acidic but not change its color, says Watnick. But some can change the color of urine or make it exceptionally bright. B vitamins (like riboflavin) can turn it fluorescent yellow, rhubarb a reddish-brown, and beets a festive pink.

Anything but the usual yellow – including Mountain-Dew-adjacent hues – may signal your body is consuming something it can’t use. “If you get super fluorescent or super red, you’re eating too much of something or taking too many supplements,” says Moe.

For most healthy people, urine color changes are rarely an emergency. Notable exceptions include people with kidney disease, or if the color change is accompanied by other concerning symptoms like new pain, a new rash or severe leg swelling. These types of changes might signify a medical problem – get it checked out.

Otherwise, to troubleshoot a strange new urine hue, first stop any supplements you’re taking, says Moe. If it doesn’t go back to normal, cut out brightly colored foods next.

Additionally, look over your medication list. If you recently started a new drug, ask your clinician whether it could cause urine color changes. But don’t stop taking any prescribed medicines before that conversation, as urinary changes are an expected and harmless side-effect of some drugs.

If your urine is red or brown, you haven’t had any red flag symptoms, and the color persists after you’ve ruled out any recent dietary or medication changes, get checked out.

Bleeding in the kidneys, the bladder or the urinary tract can also turn it red or brown, and your clinician can assess that with a simple urine test. (In people who menstruate, it can occasionally be challenging to determine where blood in the toilet is coming from. Talk to your clinician if you’re not sure.)

Foamy urine can mean protein is leaking from your kidneys – a few bubbles aren’t worrying, but you should be concerned if you see anything that looks “like a beer head in the toilet”, says Moe.

Odor, frequency and transparency are also important. A sweet or foul smell, peeing much more or less than usual, and cloudy urine are all reasons to get checked.

Although urine changes can occasionally herald kidney problems, most kidney disease is invisible; 37 million US adults have chronic kidney disease, but only one in 10 of them is aware. Moe says the best prevention is keeping your blood pressure in a healthy range and eating lots of fruits and vegetables, with meat in moderation. “The carnivore diet is not a healthy diet,” she says.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: England frustrated; Scotland face Brazil; Infantino defends hydration breaks – live
articles.summary: ⚽ All the latest news on a day packed with six matches ⚽ Player guide | Bracketology | Golden Boot | Mail Daniel How do we feel about the penalty that wasn’t? I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too. Continue reading...
articles.content:
At the start of the competition, it didn’t look like a 1-0 win and two one-goal defeats would be enough for Scotland, but now, that seems likely to qualify them. However, Brazil looked much better in their second game than their first – admittedly against far worse opposition, but it did also look like Carlo Ancelotti is clover to finding his best team. Against Morocco, I was shocked to see Igor Thiago selected ahead of Matheus Cunha; I think we can safely say that will not happen again.

Which I guess brings us to our next round of action. Before we properly dig in, let’s acquaint ourselves with the panoply of permutations.

Colombia played pretty well, I thought, and would’ve won by more were it not for Lionel Mpasi in the DRC net. I was disappointed by the winner because on first look, I thought Daniel Muñoz had done him with the eyes, but it turned out to be a deflection.

Panama have come on loads since England clattered them in 2018 – Ghana also got away with it against them. Luka Modric, though, what a player.

Qatar’s manager, Julen Lopetegui, has revealed Assim Madibo spent the eve of their final Group A match visiting Ismael Kone after the Canada midfielder underwent successful surgery for a broken leg.

Madibo was sent off after inadvertently injuring Kone in last week’s 6-0 defeat to Canada. At the time Madibo was visibly distraught and he has since visited Kone in Vancouver, Canada’s base for the tournament. Kone, who plays in Serie A for Sassuolo, is expected to miss at least five months of action. “It has been very tough for him,” Lopetegui said of Madibo on Tuesday afternoon. “We wish him [Kone] all the best to recover as soon as possible. “Now in the current moment Madibo is in Vancouver visiting Kone because he was very, very affected by this injury – it was never his intention. It was a very clear accident. We wish him all the best.” Madibo is suspended for Qatar’s match against Bosnia and Herzegovina in Seattle on Wednesday. Homam Ahmed is also suspended after being sent off in the same game last Thursday.

Iran prepared for their final Group G match by highlighting the US’s deadly attack on a school that killed at least 168 people, predominantly schoolchildren. Iran’s players trained at their base in Tijuana, Mexico, on Tuesday evening with black corner flags adorned with the message: “#168” . The number refers to the victims who were killed in a strike on an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran. The attack was attributed to the US military, with Donald Trump last week saying: “Nobody did that on purpose. Mistakes are made. The war is nasty.” When Iran first landed at their base in Mexico earlier this month, after a training camp in Turkey, they arrived wearing pin badges on their lapels that read: “#168”. Iran will arrive in Seattle from Tijuana at 11.30am local time on Wednesday before facing Egypt on Friday after being granted special permission to arrive in the US two days before the game. The match is the World Cup’s designated Pride Match, despite both teams complaining to Fifa about the celebrations which will coincide with Seattle’s Pride weekend. After Sunday’s draw with Belgium, Iran left a handwritten note in the dressing room at Los Angeles Stadium in which they called for peace. The message, which also featured #168, read: ““From the ancient Persia of thousands of years ago to the civilised Iran of today, the spirit of Iran remains alive and steadfast. We came to Los Angeles with pride, competed with honour, and leave with dignity “Thank you Los Angeles for your hospitality. And thank you to every Iranian who gave their heart, voice and soul for Iran throughout these 180 minutes. May peace, respect and friendship prevail among all nations.”

Fifa’s view of Iran training with #168 flags remains to be seen. Their regulations state that “equipment must not have any political, religious or personal slogans, statements or images” or players and/or the team may be sanctioned by the competition organiser.

Iran were only permitted to arrive in LA before draws against New Zealand and Belgium 24 hours before the games, leading their head coach, Amir Ghalenoei to label Iran the “most oppressed” team at the tournament.

Also at training on Tuesday, the former Brighton winger Alireza Jahanbakshsh was given a commemorative Iran shirt after reaching 100 caps for his country against Belgium. Fifa has been contacted for comment.

I don’t want to get all conspiracist, but you don’t have be John Le Carré to wonder if TV companies benefitting from ad revenue has an upside for Fifa even though they’re not cut in on each specific deal.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has defended the introduction of hydration breaks at the World Cup , insisting that for football’s ⁠governing body they are driven purely by sporting considerations and not commercial interests.

This has fuelled debate over their impact on the game, with some viewers complaining about ⁠being exposed to commercials during the three-minute stoppages.

“There is no additional revenue for Fifa, as all ​commercial agreements were signed well in advance. ‌So, this is not ‌a financial issue for us. For us, it is purely a sporting matter,” Infantino said in ‌a statement on Wednesday.

The breaks allow coaching staff to give in-game tactical instructions, a shift critics say disrupts match momentum and fundamentally alters the nature of the game.

England manager Thomas Tuchel said the additional break “interrupts and changes the identity of the football match“, while Uruguay coach Marcelo Bielsa said dividing matches into shorter segments takes away the fundamental characteristic ‌of the game.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Netherlands captain Virgil van Dijk have supported the intent behind the rule in extreme heat, but questioned ​the need for it in cooler conditions and at covered venues.

“The main reason is the heat, but we also have to understand that in a competition like the (FIFA) World Cup, played over 39 days, with teams potentially playing eight matches in those 39 days, having a moment to rest ⁠is extremely important,” Infantino said.

“What matters even more to us is ensuring ​that all teams, in every ​match, are playing under the ​same conditions.

“It’s very difficult to accept that a coach might have the opportunity ​to influence a ‌match by making adjustments ​simply because it’s ​hotter, while in another match, where the temperature is slightly lower, the same coach doesn’t have the same opportunity.”

Infantino added that the breaks had not reduced the intensity of matches, suggesting players were able to maintain a high level of performance throughout games.

“Is it possible we all got over excited by England beating an old and possibly quite poor Croatia team (who laboured to a 1-0 win over Panama)?” wonders Samuel Dodson. “Tuchel’s record against any reasonable side seems to be losses against Japan and Senegal and a draw against another ailing once-decent side in Uruguay. Friendlies don’t really matter, of course; and that second half surge for 15 minutes really was very fun. And not very much like how we expect England to play. This stodgy draw against Ghana however is exactly how I expect England to play. Remember 0-0 against Algeria? The USA? The good news of course is that the performance and result means we can go back to what we do best – endless debate and faux controversy and anger over team selections. Had we beaten Ghana comfortably here in not sure we or the media would have quite known how to react or what to talk about.”

Croatia definitely played into England’s hands, but the way they took control of the game was impressive. Watching it, my sense was that at some point, the defence would let them down, and Japan are a particularly difficult opponent for how they’re trying to play – so too Spain – but on a good day they can beat anyone and even on a bad day, they’ve the attacking talent to save themselves. Do I think they’re likely champions? No, but I don’t think it’s impossible.

Remember 2018, when Emmanuel Macron got drenched as Vladimir Putin relaxed under an umbrella held for him? How will Trump assert himself to this level?

I was really disappointed with Reece James. He’s a superb player capable of so much better going forward and England really needed that from him – overlaps, underlaps and crosses. But he delivered almost nothing.

Email! “‘I don’t care about Messi’ was such an insulting and insensitive remark from such a talented player,” says Krishnamoorthy V of Ronaldo. “This is what ego does to your personality. Ghana sending CR7 and co home will be so satisfying.”

I think that imperviousness has made Ronaldo what he is. Of course, he’s not really impervious at all, but thinks he is, and that’s all that matters.

Jacob makes a fair point here, that Palmer and Foden didn’t do enough to force their way into the squad. But both are special talents who’ve shown quality miles beyond that which we’ve seen from Madueke and Gordon, who are not, and neither of whom were all that good last season either.

Again, though, I come back to the big-space/small-space thing, and the lack of balance in the squad. And, judging by the substitutions, it’s not something management see as an issue – the changes were like for like, rather than seeking to alter or vary the method of attack.

The good news for England is that, as they progress, teams will, most likely, look to attack them, leaving space for their speed and physicality to exploit. But the squad lack guile and magic, completely unnecessarily, and it’s not clear Tuchel really groks that.

Anderson, Rice and Bellingham are all fantastic players, but none have the deftness around the box to play quick combinations, or the eye to thread through little passes. It was obvious at half-time that, given what was available, the wise move was to hook one of the first two for Kobbie Mainoo, who is brilliant at finding space in traffic.

Or, in other words, a balanced midfield is not three power-players; at least one touch-player is required, and Mainoo is the only one England have. Perhaps you might say Eberechi Eze is that too, and he came on far too late to influence the game or for it to look like the coaching staff are on top of the problem.

I agree with Barney here: this was a small-space game, in which England used big-space players.

Partly this is because of the squad Thomas Tuchel picked. If I was facing England and you offered me Noni Madueke, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden, I know which of those three I’d back myself against. Madueke is a decent player, but no more than that; he isn’t special, and the other two are.

Palmer, in particular, has the ability to change the pace of a game and do surprising things others can’t, exactly what you need against an organised low block. But that wast the only glaring issue: Lewis Hall would’ve given England natural width on the left and also excellent passing out of defence, but he’s not even in the squad; and, though Trent Alexander-Arnold is no one’s idea of a proper defender, if you’re using him it’s because you need a goal, and leaving his delivery and craft at home makes absolutely no sense.

I wonder if these errors reflect a manager unfamiliar with tournament football; Tuchel has decided to play a particular way, and picked a collection of profiles he thinks can do that. But that’s left him without the means to change things properly; if things go wrong, he can swap players, but what if, as yesterday, the issue is the system and its principles?

I feel not. Had Fatawu got a touch on the ball, Pickford was toast, but because neither player did, I don’t think we can say there was a foul. Both went for it, both missed, so it makes most sense is to call it a collision.

I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too.

As far as goalless draws go, I thought it an engaging one. But plenty of things for Thomas Tuchel to ponder, which we’ll dig into into which we’ll dig presently.

This “I’m back” situation, though; it’ll take more than bagging a brace against Uzbekistan for that to be so.

Roberto Martínez has options, too. He could play a wide player up front – Pedro Neto has done it for Chelsea – or Goncalo Ramos, who’s a striker.

But it’s not just Ronaldo preventing this team from working as it should – Bernardo Silva was left out and, if they’re to fulfil their potential – they’ve got the players to win the thing – he must surely play a key role. I’d get him into a midfield three with Vitinha and João Neves, then have Bruno Fernandes and Neto with free roles behind – if we must – Ronaldo.

Surely no one rhose surname isn’t Dos Santos Aveiro really thinks that, though? Ronaldo can still finish – he’ll never lose that – but it’s very hard to even come up with rationale, never mind believe rationale, that says the best version of this Portugal team contains him.

We go again! We’ll begin by reflecting on the latest action – Portugal getting their competition going by thrashing Uzbekistan, England and Ghana near-enough securing passage to the knockouts, Croatia just about seeing off Panama, now eliminated, and Colombia forcing their way past DR Congo.

Then, when we’ve done that, we’ll build up to today’s action, featuring the final round of matches in Group B – Switzerland v Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina v Qatar; Group C – Morocco v Haiti and Scotland v Brazil… and Group A – South Africa v South Korea and Czechia v México.

I reckon some people might have some thoughts about all of that lot, so we’ll share those of our writers, but do send in yours too.
